# Sensitivity Oracles for Matroid Packing, Matroid Covering, and Matching Problems with Applications Keerti Choudhary∗
Amit Kumar†
Lakshay Saggi‡ **Abstract** Sensitivity oracles preprocess a graph so that queries can be answered after any _f_ edge insertions and deletions, without recomputing from scratch. For structural optimization problems the known landscape is limited: for flows and cuts, all known compact oracles handle only \(f\le 2\) failures; existing oracles for _s_- and global min-cut apply only to undirected graphs; and for matchings, arborescence and spanning-tree packings, and arboricity, no efficient oracle is known for _f\>_1. We present a unified algebraic framework based on sensitivity oracles for matroid packing, covering, and parity of sparse linear matroids, yielding the first oracles supporting an arbitrary number _f_ of updates across all of these problems (all constructions randomized Monte-Carlo). Concretely, we obtain efficient oracles for exact (_s,t_)-max-flow/min-cut, resolving an open problem of Baswana, Bhanja, and Pandey (ICALP’22) with near-optimal space; for all-pairs _k_- bounded flow, generalizing the near-optimal reachability oracle of Brand and Saranurak (FOCS’19, the case _k=_1); the first oracles for any _f_ for directed _s_- and global min-cut; oracles for _k_-disjoint arborescences, _k_-disjoint spanning trees, colorful spanning trees, and arboricity; and oracles for the existence of an \(\alpha\)-factor, with perfect matching as the case \(\alpha=1\). We further introduce the _subset sensitivity model_, in which updates are confined to a susceptible edge set of size \(\sigma\) fixed during preprocessing. Here we decouple updates from the matroid representation and eliminate the dependence on _k_ and the matroid density altogether: all of the above are supported with \(\widetilde{O}(f\omega)\) query time and \(O(f\sigma^2)\) space. We also prove a matching \(\Omega(min\{\sigma^2,n^2\})\)-bit lower bound when \(f\ge 2\), establishing optimality. ∗Department of Computer Science and Engineering, IIT Delhi, India. ## 1 Introduction

Real-world networks, including communication, transportation, and infrastructure networks, are inherently subject to failures and transient perturbations. Links may fail, capacities may fluctuate, and new connections may be introduced.

This motivates the study of _sensitivity oracles_ (also called fault-tolerant oracles): compact data structures that preprocess a graph (or a more general combinatorial object) so that, for any small set of _f_ updates (edge insertions, deletions, or weight changes), queries about the updated object can be answered without recomputation. Over the past two decades, the sensitivity setting has been studied extensively for shortest paths and distances \[DTCR08, DP09, WY13, vdBS19, CC20, GW19, GR21, KS23a\], reachability \[BCR16, Cho16, vdBS19\], and connectivity \[PT07, DP09, BCR16, LS22\].

In contrast, the landscape is starkly different for _structural optimization_ problems such as maxflows and min-cuts, arborescence and spanning-tree packings, matchings and degree-constrained subgraphs, and matroid intersection or parity. Here, essentially all known oracles handle only \(f\le 2\) failures, and the underlying combinatorial techniques appear inherently tied to small values of _f_:

• For a fixed pair (_s,t_), Baswana, Bhanja, and Pandey \[BBP22\] designed an (_s,t_)-min-cut oracle for \(f\le 2\) edge failures with _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) space and _O_(1) query time, using the submodularity structure of minimum and near-minimum cuts, and posed the case _f\>_2 as an open problem. Recently, the authors in \[ACP<sup>+</sup>26\] handled general _f_ via directed flow augmentation \[KKPW22\], but with space and query time scaling as \(2^{O_f(\lambda^4logk)}\) in the flow value \(\lambda\), which is quite expensive for graphs with large cuts or multiple failures. For \(f\ge 3\) the relevant minimum cuts interact in increasingly complex ways, and no compact oracle avoiding this exponential dependence is known.

• For all-pairs min-cut, the only known result is the single-failure oracle of Baswana and Pandey \[BP22\]; for _s_-min-cut and global min-cut, oracles are known only for \(f\le 2\) and only in undirected graphs \[DN95, Bha25\]; in directed graphs nothing non-trivial is known.

• For matchings, degree-constrained subgraphs (\(\alpha\)-factors), disjoint arborescences, colorful spanning trees, arboricity, and matroid packing/covering/parity, no sensitivity oracles were known for any _f\>_1, even though the _dynamic_ versions of some of these problems have received attention in the past \[BMNT23, dVG26, GP13, BS15, BS16, dVC26, BKSW23, Kis23, ABR24, Beh23\], along with results about fault-tolerant subgraphs \[AB19, BGRS22, BCDW24\].

Even seemingly simple decision questions like _does the graph remain strongly connected after f updates? does it still admit a perfect matching?_ had no efficient answer. This raises the following central question of this paper:

Is there a unifying technique that yields compact, efficient sensitivity oracles, for an arbitrary number f of updates, across a vast class of structural optimization problems?

We answer this question affirmatively, and our route is _algebraic_. Algebraic techniques involving maintaining determinants and inverses of symbolic matrices under low-rank updates have recently proven remarkably effective for dynamic and fault-tolerant variants of shortest paths and reachability \[San05, WY13, vdBS19, GR21, KS23a\], dynamic matchings \[vdBNS19, vdBKZ26\], dynamic SCC \[KS23b\] along with many other applications \[vdB21\]. Yet no general framework for _sensitivity_ oracles for matroid problems has previously been studied. We bridge this gap: rather than solving each graph problem separately, we design sensitivity oracles for the fundamental matroid primitives that underlie them all: _matroid packing_, _matroid covering_, and _matroid matching (parity)_.

## 1.1 Our Contributions

Let _M_<sub>1</sub>_,M_<sub>2</sub> be two linear matroids of rank _r_ on a common ground set _E_ of size _m_, with integer element weights in \[-_W,W_\]. Given \(k\ge 1\), the _k-packing_ problem asks whether there is a set \(S\subseteq E\) of size _kr_ that can be partitioned into _k_ pairwise disjoint common bases of _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub> (the two partitions may differ); the weighted version asks for the minimum weight of such a set. The _k- covering_ problem asks whether the entire ground set can be partitioned into _k_ independent sets of a given matroid. In the _general sensitivity model_, the oracle must support up to _f_ arbitrary element updates (insertions, deletions, or weight changes) anywhere in the ground set.

For _sparse_ linear matroids (constant many non-zeros per column of the linear representation), we obtain the following.

Instantiating this framework, and combining it with new problem-specific reductions, yields the first sensitivity oracles supporting an arbitrary number _f_ of updates for a broad range of problems.

### All-pairs Bounded Flow.

For directed unit-capacity graphs with costs in \[-_W,W_\] and a flow bound _k_, we obtain an oracle that, for any pair (_s,t_) and any _f_ edge updates, report \(min(k,\lambda_{G+U}(s,t))\) in \(O((fk^2)^\omega logk)\) time, where \(\lambda_{G+U}(s,t)\) denotes the value of (_s,t_)-max-flow in the updated graph. Further, the oracle identifies the nearest (_s,t_) min-cut and computes the minimum cost of the corresponding flow, when \(\lambda_{G+U}(s,t)<k\) (see  2). Our result extends the reachability and distance sensitivity oracles of Brand and Saranurak \[vdBS19\] (the special case _k_=1), which are known to be near-optimal for constant _f_; for _k\>_1 no comparable oracles were known even for undirected graphs, where the state of the art was the single-failure all-pairs min-cut oracle of \[BP22\].

### Fixed-pair (_s,t_)-max-flow.

Our most notable application is for a fixed source-sink pair with _arbitrary_ flow value. Applying the all-pairs oracle with _k=n_ would be unnecessarily expensive; instead we present a flow-rerouting reduction whose effective capacity bound is _k=O(f_), thereby eliminating the blowup associated with large flow values. After any _f_ updates the oracle outputs the updated flow value in just \(O(f^{3\omega})\) time (see  2).

This fully resolves the open problem of Baswana, Bhanja, and Pandey \[BBP22\] for every _f_. Moreover, the space is essentially optimal for any constant \(f\ge 2\) due to \(\Omega(n^2)\) space lower bound by Bhanja \[Bha24\]. In contrast with \[ACP<sup>+</sup>26\], whose bounds degrade as 2<sup>_O<sub>f</sub>(k_<sup>4</sup>log_k_)</sup>, our bounds are polynomial in _f_ and independent of _k_.

### _s_-min-cut and global min-cut in directed graphs.

No non-trivial sensitivity oracles were known for these problems in directed graphs; undirected results \[DN95, Bha25\] existed for \(f\le 2\). We present the first directed _s_-min-cut and global min-cut oracles for arbitrary _f_ with _O(f_<sup>2</sup>_n_<sup>3</sup>log_n_) space and \(\widetilde{O}(f^{3\omega+1})\) query time. Additionally, the oracle reports the corresponding cut in \(\widetilde{O}(f^{3\omega} n)\) time. Further, we provide \(\Omega(n^2)\) lower bound for these problems, for any constant \(f\ge 2\). ## Spanning structures.

Our framework also yields sensitivity oracles for a broad class of spanning structure problems. As a basic example, consider the problem of deciding whether _G_ admits a reachability tree rooted at _s_ after _f_ updates. Existing pairwise reachability oracle of Brand and Saranurak \[vdBS19\] require \(\Omega(n)\) queries<sup>1</sup> to certify this property, and with query time depending only on _f_ was previously not known. We instead obtain an oracle for deciding the existence of _k_ edge-disjoint arborescences rooted at a _query_ root _s_ in \(O((fk^2)^\omega)\) time. Instantiating _k_=1 yields an \(O(f^\omega)\)-time oracle for rooted reachability trees.

As an immediate consequence, since _k_-strong connectivity amounts to existence of _k_-arborescence packing in both directions from any root, we decide _k_-strong connectivity of _G+U_ in \(O((fk^2)^\omega)\) time with _O_((_kn_)<sup>2</sup>log_n_) space (Theorem 5.4). For comparison, for _k_=1, the oracle of \[BCR19\] reports the strongly connected components after _f_ failures using _O_(2_<sup>f</sup>n_<sup>2</sup>) space and \(\widetilde{O}(2^fn)\) query time; for the decision problem we replace both exponential dependencies by poly(_f_).

The same guarantees extend to deciding the existence of _k_ edge-disjoint spanning trees. We also obtain the first sensitivity oracle for colorful (rainbow) spanning trees, with \(O(f^\omega)\) query time and quadratic space, and additionally provide a matching lower bound on the oracle size. Finally, we give the first sensitivity oracle for deciding whether the updated graph has arboricity (the minimum number of forests needed to cover edges of a graph) at most _k_, answering queries in \(O((fk)^\omega)\) time (see  3).

For degree bounds \(\alpha(v)\unknown k\), this yields an \(\alpha\)-factor existence oracle with _O_((_kn_)<sup>2</sup>log_n_) space and \(O((fk^2)^\omega)\) query time. As a special case, setting \(\alpha=1\) gives a perfect matching oracle with _O(n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_) space and \(O(f^\omega)\) query time. We complement this with an \(\Omega(n^2)\) space lower bound for perfect matching oracles for \(f\unknown 2\) updates, establishing space optimality up to logarithmic factors. Handling _arbitrary_ degree bounds requires a different approach: the standard expansion is prohibitively large, and unlike maximum flow, \(\alpha\)-factors admit no natural residual graph. We develop a residual-graph analogue based on closed alternating trails in the symmetric difference of two \(\alpha\)-factors, yielding an oracle with _O_((_fn_)<sup>2</sup>log_n_) space and \(O(f^{3\omega})\) query time, independent of \(max_v\alpha(v)\).

The dependence on _k_ arises from our generic reduction, which maps _f_ updates in the original instance to \(\Theta(fk^2)\) updates in the auxiliary matrix representation on which our framework operates. This leads to a natural question: can one eliminate the dependence on _k_ and obtain query time depending only on the number _f_ of updates?

_Can the dependence on k (and on the matroid density) be removed from the query time altogether, possibly at the cost of more but still polynomial space?_

## Removing the dependence on _k_, and Subset Sensitivity.

We answer this question affirmatively. The _k_-dependence in the general model arises because every update modifies the oracle’s internal matroid representation, and the cost of each such modification grows with _k_. Our key idea is to _decouple updates from the representation_. The price of decoupling is space, which now scales with the square of the set of elements that may ever be added or deleted, which in the worst case is _O(m_<sup>2</sup>).

Additionally, we observe that if the set of edge updates is restricted to a smaller set of size \(\sigma\), then the space of our oracle has only a quadratic dependence on \(\sigma\). We therefore introduce the _subset sensitivity model_, where, a set _E<sub>Q</sub>_ of _susceptible_ elements of size \(\sigma\), possibly including elements not initially present, is specified at preprocessing time, and all updates are restricted to _E<sub>Q</sub>_. This captures applications where changes are localized, such as a known set of vulnerable links or candidate edges, and reduces the space requirement to \(O(\sigma^2)\).

## 1.2 Technical Overview

We now describe the main ideas underlying our framework. To illustrate the key techniques, we develop our algebraic approach through the lens of the (_s,t_)-max-flow sensitivity oracle. We first restrict attention to the decision (unweighted) versions; the weighted versions follow naturally by introducing an indeterminate _Y_ whose exponents encode weights. Throughout, \(\omega\) is the matrix multiplication exponent and F is a sufficiently large finite field.

### 1.2.1 From Reachability to _k_-Bounded Flow

Consider the problem of preprocessing a directed graph _G_ such that for any query consisting of a subset of _f_ edge updates, the updated (_s,t_)-max-flow value can be quickly reported. Prior sensitivity oracles for cuts and flows have been predominantly combinatorial \[BBP22, ACP<sup>+</sup>26, BP22\]. These methods analyze the structure of minimum and near-minimum (_s,t_)-cuts and how failures interact with them. While successful for small _f_, this analysis becomes increasingly intricate as the number of failures grows, causing query times or space to blow up exponentially with the flow value \[ACP<sup>+</sup>26\].

We instead take an algebraic approach. Our starting point is the work of Brand and Saranurak \[vdBS19\], who obtained reachability and distance sensitivity oracles for any number of failures. _Can this algebraic paradigm be lifted from reachability (k_=1_) to k-bounded flow-- deciding whether at least k edge-disjoint_ (_s,t)-paths survive f edge updates?_

We answer this question by building a general algebraic framework based on matroids.

## Modeling Flow as Matroid Intersection.

Given a directed graph _H_=(_V<sub>H</sub>,E<sub>H</sub>_) with designated terminals _s_ and _t_, we can encode the existence of exactly \(\lambda\) edge-disjoint (_s,t_)-paths as a matroid intersection problem. We first augment _H_ by adding exactly _k_ zero-cost self-loops at every vertex \(v\in V_H\backslash\{s,t\}\), and \(k-\lambda\) zero-cost self-loops at _s_ and _t_. We then define two partition matroids on this augmented edge set:

• _M_<sub>out</sub>: A subset \(S\subseteq E_H\) is independent if every vertex \(v\in V_H\backslash\{t\}\) has at most one outgoing edge in _S_.<tbc>

• _M_<sub>in</sub>: A subset \(S\subseteq E_H\) is independent if every vertex \(v\in V_H\backslash\{s\}\) has at most one incoming edge in _S_.

A common basis of _M_<sub>out</sub> and _M_<sub>in</sub> is a subset _S_ that satisfies both degree constraints tightly. Combinatorially, such a set _S_ forces the existence of exactly \(\lambda\) edge-disjoint (_s,t_)-paths, with the self-loops absorbing the remaining degree budget at each vertex. Furthermore, a minimum-weight common basis corresponds exactly to the minimum-cost routing of these paths.

To test for _k_-bounded flow, we must check if the graph can support the packing of _k_ such structures. This is equivalent to checking if the ground set _E<sub>H</sub>_ contains a subset that can be partitioned into _k_ common bases of _M_<sub>out</sub> and _M_<sub>in</sub>.

Our resolution to this is to pass to _k-fold unions_. The _k_-fold union \(M^{\vee k}\) of a matroid _M_ is a matroid whose independent sets are the union of _k_ independent sets of _M_. Because partition matroids are strongly base-orderable, checking for a _k_-packing of common bases is perfectly equivalent to checking for a _single_ common basis of the _k_-fold unions \(M_\mathrm{out}^{\vee k}\) and \(M_\mathrm{in}^{\vee k}\).

To represent these unions algebraically, we use the randomized construction of Narayanan, Saran and Vazirani \[NSV94\]. If a linear matroid _M_ of rank _r_ has a representation matrix \(A\in\mathbb{F}^{r\times m}\), its _k_-fold union \(M^{\vee k}\) can be represented by stacking _k_ copies of _A_, each scaled column-wise by a random diagonal matrix _C<sub>i</sub>_:

\(U=\big(AC_1;AC_2;\dots;AC_k\big)\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times m}\)

Let _U_<sub>out</sub> and _U_<sub>in</sub> be the \(kr\times m\) union representation matrices for \(M_\mathrm{out}^{\vee k}\) and \(M_\mathrm{in}^{\vee k}\). We associate a formal variable _Y_ and an independent random scalar _x<sub>e</sub>_ with each element _e_, forming a diagonal weight matrix \(D\in\mathbb{F}[Y]^{m\times m}\) where _D<sub>e,e</sub>=x<sub>e</sub>Y_<sup>_W_+**_wt_**(_e_)</sup>.

Then the _mixed Laplacian_ is defined as:

\(\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{pack}=U_\mathrm{out}DU_\mathrm{in}^T\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times kr}\)

By a _k_-fold Cauchy-Binet expansion, the determinant of L<sub>pack</sub> enumerates the common bases of the unions. _Thus, k-bounded flow is reduced entirely to evaluating whether_ \(\mathrm{det}(\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{pack})\neq 0\) _(for existence) and isolating its minimum Y-degree (for minimum cost)._

## Sensitivity via Sparse Determinant Updates.

The power of this formulation in the sensitivity setting lies in sparsity. An update to an edge _e_ in the graph only modifies the _e_-th rank-one term in the Laplacian sum \(\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{pack}=\sum_{e\in E}D_{e,e}(u_\mathrm{out})_e(u_\mathrm{in})_e^T\). Because the base partition matroids are extremely sparse (_O_(1) non-zeros per column), the union columns (_u_<sub>out</sub>)_<sub>e</sub>_ and (_u_<sub>in</sub>)_<sub>e</sub>_ have at most _O(k_) non-zeros. Consequently:

_Any f edge updates in the graph translate to a sparse additive update to_ L<sub>pack</sub> _containing only O(fk_<sup>2</sup>) _non-zero entries._

To evaluate this perturbed determinant, we utilize the Matrix Determinant Lemma, which allows us to compute the determinant of a matrix under a low-rank update in time proportional to the update size, provided we have precomputed its inverse. We leverage the data structure of Brand and Saranurak \[vdBS19\] to achieve this.

_Remark on Singular Matrices:_ The original tool of \[vdBS19\] required the base matrix L<sub>pack</sub> to be invertible (i.e., the base graph must already possess the required flow). We remove this limitation by introducing a random low-rank numeric pad _UV<sup>T</sup>_ during preprocessing that forces invertibility. When a query arrives, we fold the numeric pad back into the query update as a structured low-rank perturbation (Theorem A.2), allowing the determinant lemma to work seamlessly even if the base matrix is identically singular.

With this tool, an _f_-edge update can be evaluated in \(O((fk^2)^\omega)\) time for the decision version, and \(\widetilde{O}(Wkr(fk^2)^\omega)\) time for the weighted version.

### Extension to All-Pairs queries via Parallel Elements.

To extend this to dynamic all-pairs \((V\times V)\) queries without blowing up the matrix dimension, we introduce a static dummy source _s_<sup>∗</sup> and dummy sink _t_<sup>∗</sup> during preprocessing. At query time, to test (_s,t_)-flow, we dynamically insert _k_ parallel edges from _s_<sup>∗</sup> to _s_ and from _t_ to _t_<sup>∗</sup>. Crucially, parallel copies of an edge share the exact same sparse column support in the base matroid representations. Thus, adding _k_ parallel edges only perturbs an \(O(k)\times O(k)\) block in the Laplacian-contributing _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) modified entries, exactly the same cost as a _single_ edge update. Therefore, an all-pairs query with _f_ updates costs \(O((fk^2+k^2)^\omega)=O((fk^2)^\omega)\) time, rather than a naive multiplicative blowup of \(O(((f+k)k^2)^\omega)\).

## 1.2.2 Two Strategies for Exact (_s,t_)-Max-Flow

The bounded flow oracle performs well for small flow values, whereas extending it to exact, unbounded (_s,t_)-max-flow remains challenging. In particular, setting _k=n_ in the all-pairs oracle leads to extremely slow query time.

We develop two distinct strategies to resolve this: one focusing on algorithmic rerouting, and the other on structurally decoupling the matrix updates.

### Strategy 1: Residual Graph Reduction

Here we consider the question if recomputing the exact flow value after _f_ edge updates can be reduced to All-pairs bounded flow problem. Our core insight is that _sensitivity does not require computing the entire flow, only repairing it_.

During preprocessing, we compute an exact max-flow _h_ of value \(\lambda_G(s,t)\). Consider a set of edge failures _F_, of which \(d\le f\) edges actually carried flow in _h_. Deleting these _d_ edges destroys exactly _d_ units of flow, leaving _d_ units of excess at the severed tail vertices and _d_ units of deficit at the head vertices.

To repair the flow, we must re-route these _d_ units of excess to the deficits. This is equivalent to finding _d_ edge-disjoint paths in the _residual graph_ (_G-F)<sub>h</sub>_. By attaching a dummy source to the excess vertices and a dummy sink to the deficit vertices, repairing the exact max-flow is reduced completely to an all-pairs bounded-flow query on the residual graph with an effective capacity bound of \(k=d\le f\).

To support insertions and accurately track the new flow value, we pad the base graph _G_ with 2_f_ zero-cost parallel (_s,t_)-buffer edges, saturating _f_ of them in _h_. Insertions and deletions simply<tbc>

force the repaired flow to saturate fewer or more of these buffer edges, allowing us to obtain the new max-flow value \(\lambda_{G+U}(s,t)\) directly off the buffer usage via binary search (Theorem 4.3).

By plugging this residual graph formulation back into our all-pairs bounded flow oracle with _k=O(f_), we drop the global capacity _n_ from the query time entirely. This resolves the open problem of \[BBP22\] by yielding an exact max-flow oracle bounded purely by \(\widetilde{O}(f^{3\omega})\) query time and _O_((_fn_)<sup>2</sup>log_n_) space. Costs are handled seamlessly by tracking the cost of the rerouting paths in the residual graph (Theorem 4.4).

### Strategy 2: The Subset Sensitivity Model (Decoupling)

While the residual rerouting strategy successfully removed _k_ from the query time, the query time still turns out to be \(O(f^{3\omega})\). This leads to a second question:

_Can we remove the dependence on k from the algebraic update time directly, maintaining an_ \(O(f^\omega)\) _query cost while simultaneously shrinking the space requirement?_

The algebraic bottleneck in the general model occurs because every physical edge update forces the oracle to explicitly rewrite _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) entries in the dense union representation.

We resolve this by _decoupling the updates from the representations_. We _freeze_ the representation matrices _A_:=_U_<sub>out</sub> and _B_:=_U_<sub>in</sub> at preprocessing. Instead of updating the matroids directly, we realize every network update as a simple _diagonal switch_ in the weight matrix _D_. An element is either toggled on, off, or reweighted. For an update set \(S\subseteq Q\) of size _f_, the query matrix becomes:<tbc>

\(L'=AD'B^T=L+A_S\Delta_SB_S^T\)

<tbc>and by Theorem 2.3,<tbc>

\(det(L')=det(L)\cdot det\big(I_f+B_S^TL^{-1}A_S\Delta_S\big).\)

<tbc>The only data a query needs is the \(f\times f\) matrix \(B_S^TL^{-1}A_S\). Interestingly, we observe that if the locus of edge updates is confined to a _susceptible set Q_ of size \(\sigma\) declared at preprocessing, then it suffices to compute and store the \(\sigma\times\sigma\) principal submatrix

\(U_Q:=B_Q^TL^{-1}A_Q.\)

This allows us to also introduce the **Subset Sensitivity Model**, where a susceptible set of elements _Q_ (of size \(\sigma\)) is designated at preprocessing time. We thus obtain the following result.

**Lemma 1.1** (Subset determinant oracle; see Theorem A.1)**.** _Let_ \(A,B\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{r\times m}\)_, let D be diagonal, L=ADB<sup>T</sup> (possibly singular), and let_ \(Q\subseteq[m]\), \(|Q|=\sigma\)_, be fixed at preprocessing. There is a data structure that, for any_ \(D'\) _differing from D in_ \(\le f\) _positions within Q, computes_ \(det(AD'B^T)\)_: for d_=0_, with_ \(O(\sigma^2r^{\omega-2}+r^\omega)\) _preprocessing,_ \(O(\sigma^2)\) _space, and_ \(O(f^\omega)\) _query time._

By leveraging this subset determinant lemma on our fixed (_s,t_) flow formulations, we remove the dependence on matrix dimensions and packing parameters from the query time, yielding an exact (_s,t_)-max flow oracle with an optimal \(\widetilde{O}(f^\omega)\) query time and strict \(O(\sigma^2)\) space.

## 1.2.3 Other Applications of Matroid Intersection

Our algebraic framework extends far beyond (_s,t_)-flows. We discuss some of these applications below.

### _s_-min-cut and global min-cut.

The _s_-min-cut is \(min_{v\neq s}\lambda(s,v)\); storing an (_s,v_) oracle for every _v_ makes a query _n_ evaluations, which is too slow. For _deletions only_ there is a simple fix: if the _s_-min-cut decreases, some deleted edge (_x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>i</sub>_) crosses the new minimum cut, hence the new cut separates _s_ from some _y<sub>i</sub>_; so it suffices to query the \(\le f\) sinks {_y<sub>i</sub>_}, plus compare against the old value. _Insertions break this_: the new min-cut may avoid all updated edges yet still be smaller than the old cut _would have been after insertions_, the baseline itself moves. We restore the argument with a preprocessing trick based on Frank’s augmentation approach \[Fra90\]. We compute an _optimal_ set _I_<sup>∗</sup> of _f_ edges whose insertion maximizes the _s_-min-cut, and let \(\lambda^*=\mu_{G+I^*}(s)\). For any update set _U_ (with \(|U|\le f\) insertions), \(\mu_{G+U}(s)\le\lambda^*\) by optimality of _I_<sup>∗</sup>; and if the minimum cut of _G+U_ is not crossed by any edge of \(I^*\cup U\), its capacity is identical in _G+U_ and _G+I_<sup>∗</sup>, hence at least \(\lambda^*\). Therefore, we have (Theorem 4.7)

\(\mu_{G+U}(s)=min\big(\lambda^*,min_{y\in Y,y\neq s}\lambda_{G+U}(s,y)\big),Y=\text{heads of}I^*\cup U,|Y|\le 2f,\)

reducing the query to _O(f_) fixed-pair max-flow queries against precomputed (_s,v_)-oracles. Global min-cut follows by symmetry: it equals \(min(\mu_G(s),\mu_{G^\mathrm{rev}}(s))\) for any fixed _s_.

### Spanning structures and arboricity

Arborescence packing is the second application of the same framework: by Edmonds’ theorem, _k_ disjoint _z_-rooted arborescences correspond to a _k_-packing of the graphic matroid against the in-degree partition matroid. To support a _query-time root s_, we keep an isolated dummy root _z_ at preprocessing and, at query time, insert _k_ parallel edges (_z,s_); by the cheap-parallel-elements refinement this bundle costs only _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) additional Laplacian entries.

As in (_s,t_)-max-flow scenario, the parallel copies of one element share the same sparse column support, so all _k_ copies together touch only an \(O(k)\times O(k)\) submatrix (_O(k_<sup>2</sup>) entries total), the same as a _single_ update (Theorem 3.6). Thus a query consisting of _f_ genuine updates plus a bundle of _k_ parallel query edges costs \(O((fk^2+k^2)^\omega)=O((fk^2)^\omega)\), not \(O(((f+k)k^2)^\omega)\). This observation is small but load-bearing: it is what makes _dynamic-root_ arborescence queries and _all-pairs_ flow queries as cheap as static-root ones. So a dynamic-root query is exactly as cheap as a static one with query time \(O((fk^2)^\omega)\), and \(O(f^\omega)\) for _k_=1, which is the single-source reachability-tree oracle highlighted in the introduction. Spanning-tree packing (_M_<sub>1</sub>=_M_<sub>2</sub>=graphic), colorful spanning trees (graphic vs. color-partition, _k_=1), and arboricity (_k_-covering of the graphic matroid, using the random-augmentation covering oracle) follow the same recipe with \(\delta=f\) column updates.

Arboricity (partitioning a graph into _k_ forests) is a _covering_ problem. Here the goal is to determine if the entire edge set is independent in the _k_-fold graphic union, i.e., whether the \(kr\times m\) (where _r=n_-1) representation union matrix _U_ has full column rank. We convert rank to determinant by squaring it up, appending _kr-m_ uniformly random columns _R_. A Laplace-expansion argument proves that the square matrix is non-singular, \(\mathrm{det}([U|R])\neq 0\), w.h.p. exactly when the rank is full (Theorem 3.9) and the graph is _k_-coverable. Since the random columns never change and each edge update touches _O(k_) entries, we apply our determinant oracles directly, yielding a query time of \(O((fk)^\omega)\) (Theorems 3.10 and 5.10).

## 1.2.4 Matroid Parity and \(\alpha\)-Factors

### Sparse linear matroid parity.

The parity (matroid matching) problem admits an analogous algebraic formulation: the determinant of the skew-symmetric matrix _ADB<sup>T</sup>-BDA<sup>T</sup>_ is the square of a Pfaffian enumerating parity bases (Theorem 6.1). For _c_-sparse matroids, _f_ pair updates modify _O(c_<sup>2</sup>_f_) entries, and this yields the parity oracle (Theorem 6.2), and in turn the bounded-degree \(\alpha\)-factor and perfect matching oracles.

### \(\alpha\)-factors with arbitrary degree bounds.

For arbitrary \(\alpha\), the parity instance has dimension \(\sum_v\alpha(v)\), which can be \(\Theta(nm)\). To tackle this, we fix a min-cost \(\alpha\)-factor _M_ at preprocessing; for any updated optimum \(M'\), the symmetric difference \(M\triangle M'\) decomposes into closed alternating trails. We prove two facts (i) there exists optimal \(M'\) such that the difference decomposes into at most _f_ trails; and (ii) a trail with no closed alternating sub-trail meets each vertex in at most two _M_-edges and two \(M'\)-edges (else a sub-trail could be extracted, an argument inspired by the bicoloured-cycle technique of \[FS05\]). Thus, an optimal \(\alpha\)-factor of _G+U_ drops at most 2_f_ edges of _M_ at every vertex. This local bound lets us build an auxiliary two-layer graph (a drop layer for _M_-edges, an add layer for non-_M_-edges, coupled by parallel edges and unit budget gadgets), on which factors of _G+U_ correspond exactly, with matching costs, to factors of the auxiliary graph (Theorem 7.7). The bounded-degree oracle with _k=O(f_) then gives _O_((_fn_)<sup>2</sup>log_n_) space and \(O(f^{3\omega})\) query time, independent of \(max_v\alpha(v)\) (Theorem 7.8).

## 1.3 Related Works

### Matroid Algorithms.

Polynomial-time algorithms for matroid union and intersection date back to Edmonds \[Edm03\] and Lawler \[Law75\], followed by a long line of work improving exact and approximate algorithms for matroid intersection, union, packing, and covering \[Cun86, Har09, Qua24, Ter25\]. More recently, there has been growing interest in matroid algorithms over uncertain inputs. Blikstad, Mukhopadhyay, Nanongkai, and Tu \[BMNT23\] maintain a minimum-weight basis in the decremental setting using \(\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{rank(M)})\) rank queries per update. Vos and Grilnberger \[dVG26\] gave a deterministic dynamic \((1\pm\epsilon)\)-approximation for the packing number \(\Phi\) and covering number \(\beta\) of a matroid, using \(\Phi\cdot poly(logn,1/\epsilon)\) (resp. \(\beta\cdot poly(logn,1/\epsilon)\)) rank queries per update. Sparsification techniques of Huang and Sellier \[HS24\] led to progress in streaming matroid intersection; Chandrasekaran, Chekuri, and Zhu \[CCZ25\] initiated the study of base packing in online matroids, and Buchbinder, Gupta, Hathcock, Karlin, and Sarkar \[BGH<sup>+</sup>24\] gave an \(\widetilde{O}(\text{OPT})\)-competitive algorithm for intersecting a matroid with an online partition matroid. Fault-tolerant aspects of matroids have also been studied recently \[BFGM25, DK26\].

### Static Algebraic Algorithms.

Cheung, Lau, and Leung \[CLL11\] pioneered the use of fast matrix multiplication for graph connectivity, solving All-Pairs Connectivity in \(\widetilde{O}(m^\omega)\) time. Georgiadis, Italiano, Karanasiou, Papadopoulos, and Parotsidis \[GIK<sup>+</sup>17\] presented a deterministic algorithm for all-pairs 2-bounded edge (vertex) connectivity in \(\widetilde{O}(n^\omega)\) time. Authors in \[AGI<sup>+</sup>19\] extended this to general _k_ in the vertex-capacitated setting, with a randomized \(O((nk)^\omega)\)-time algorithm; they further showed that on DAGs, all-pairs _k_-bounded max-flow can be solved in \(O((klogn)^{4^k+o(k)}\cdot n^\omega)\) time, and in \(O(2^{O(k^2)}\cdot mn)\) time for sparse DAGs. The framework of \[CLL11\] was lifted to the _k_-bounded setting (_k_-APC) by Akmal and Jin \[AJ23\] in \(\widetilde{O}((kn)^\omega)\) time, and refined by Akmal \[Akm24\] via enumerating polynomials. Analogous algebraic algorithms exist for linear matroid intersection \[Har09\], linear matroid parity \[CLL14\], and weighted \(\alpha\)-factors \[GS21a, GS21b\].

### Min-Cut Sensitivity Oracles.

Results of Picard and Queyranne \[PQ82\] and Dinitz and Vainshtein \[DV00\] imply that a single edge deletion’s effect on the (_s,t_)-max-flow value can be detected from the structure of the flow itself. For a fixed pair (_s,t_), Baswana, Bhanja, and Pandey \[BBP22\] designed the first dual-failure sensitivity oracle for (_s,t_)-min-cut, with _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) space and _O_(1) query time, and posed the design of compact oracles for more than two failures as an open problem. Very recently, Ahi, Choudhary, Pande, Pushpraj, and Saggi \[ACP<sup>+</sup>26\] constructed a max-flow sensitivity oracle for one and two failures with \(O(\lambda n)\) space and _O(n_) query time, together with an \(\Omega(n)\)<tbc>

<tbc>lower bound for \(f\ge 2\). For all-pairs single-failure min-cut, Baswana and Pandey \[BP22\] obtained an _O(n_<sup>2</sup>)-space, _O_(1)-query oracle. These combinatorial approaches exploit the structure of near- minimum cuts and flow decompositions, and appear inherently limited to one or two failures. Our framework resolves the open problem of \[BBP22\], providing the first (_s,t_)-min-cut sensitivity ora cle for any _f_, with _O_((_fn_)<sup>2</sup>log_n_) space, \(\widetilde{O}(f^{3\omega})\) query time for the value, and \(\widetilde{O}(f^{3\omega} n)\) time for reporting the nearest min-cut.

#### Fault-Tolerant Reachability and Distances.

Algebraic matrix tools have become a powerhouse for dynamic and fault-tolerant reachability and distances. Sankowski \[San04\] introduced dynamic reachability algorithms based on maintaining the inverse of a symbolic adjacency matrix. For weighted graphs, Weimann and Yuster \[WY13\] employed matrix adjoint computation for distance sensitivity, constructing an _f_-DSO with \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3-\alpha})\) space and \(\widetilde{O}(n^{2-2(1-\alpha)/f})\) query time. Brand and Saranurak \[vdBS19\] substantially improved the preprocessing and query time for multiple failures, obtaining \(\widetilde{O}(Wn^3)\) preprocessing and \(\widetilde{O}(Wnf^\omega)\) query time. Karczmarz and Sankowski \[KS23a\] recently improved multiple-failure DSOs via generic matrices and the Frobenius normal form. On the combinatorial side, \[DTCR08, BK09, DP10, CLPR12, BGLP16, Cho16, BCR17, CCFK17, DP17, GIP17, GDHI<sup>+</sup>17, GS18, BCFS21, IKP21, DR22, BCC<sup>+</sup>23, DG24\] studied the problem of designing fault-tolerant oracles for reachability, distances, and strong connectivity.

#### Dynamic Algorithms.

In the fully dynamic regime, min-cut algorithms range from Thorup’s tree-packing approach \[Tho07\] to recent expander-decomposition methods \[GHN<sup>+</sup>23, JST24\], sub- polynomial update times for all-pairs min-cuts \[JS22\], and dynamic flow advances \[VDBCK<sup>+</sup>24, vdBCK<sup>+</sup>, CKL<sup>+</sup>24, Kar24\]. Several recent works study dynamic graph algorithms with predictions \[PR23, HKP24, HSSY24, vdBFNP24, LS24, MMNS24, MMN<sup>+</sup>25\], a model related in spirit to our subset sensitivity setting.

## 2 Preliminaries

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be an uncapacitated directed graph with a cost function \(c:E\rightarrow\{-W,\dots,W\}\). A _trail P_ from edge _e_<sub>0</sub> to edge \(e_\ell\) in _G_ is a sequence of distinct edges \((e_0,e_1,\dots,e_\ell)\) with head(_e<sub>i</sub>_)=tail(_e_<sub>_i_+1</sub>) for each \(0\le i<\ell\) (vertices may repeat). The cost of a trail is the sum of its edge costs. A trail is a _path_ if no vertex repeats.

For a subset of _U_=(_I,F_) of edge updates consisting of a set _I_ of edge insertions and a set \(F\subseteq E\) of edge deletions, with \(|U|=|I|+|F|\le f\), we denote by \(G+U:=(V,(E\backslash F)\cup I)\) the graph obtained by applying the updates in _U_ to _G_.

For a pair \(s,t\in V\) , we use \(\lambda_G(s,t)\) to denote the maximum value of an (_s,t_)-flow in _G_. An (_s,t_)_-cut C_ partitions the vertex set into (_A<sub>C</sub>,B<sub>C</sub>_) with \(s\in A_C\) and \(t\in B_C\); its capacity is the number of edges directed from _A<sub>C</sub>_ to _B<sub>C</sub>_, and an (_s,t_)-min-cut is one with minimum capacity, of value \(\lambda_G(s,t)\) by the max-flow min-cut theorem. For a fixed source \(s\in V\) , the _s-min-cut_ value is<tbc>

\(\mu_G(s):=min_{v\in V\backslash\{s\}}\lambda_G(s,v)\), and the _global min-cut_ value is \(\mu_G:=min_{s\in V}\mu_G(s)\). Given an (_s,t_)-flow _h_ in _G_, the _residual graph G<sub>h</sub>_ is obtained from _G_ by reversing every edge that carries flow under _h_, i.e., replacing each edge _e_=(_u,v_) with _h(e_)=1 by its reverse _e_<sup>rev</sup>=(_v,u_), where **_c_**(_e_<sup>rev</sup>)=-**_c_**(_e_). We use val(_h_) to denote the value of the flow _h_.

An (_s,t_)-min-cut _C_<sup>∗</sup> is said to be the _nearest min-cut_ if for each (_s,t_)-min-cut _C_ we have \(A_{C^*}\subseteq A_C\). We denote such a _C_<sup>∗</sup> with NMC_<sub>G</sub>(s,t_). Ford and Fulkerson \[FF62\] gave an algorithm for constructing the (unique) nearest (_s,t_)-min-cut. For the sake of completeness we state the following characterization of NMCs from \[FF62\].

**Lemma 2.1.** _Let C=NMC<sub>G</sub>(s,t_) _with partition_ (_A,B). Then A consists precisely of those_ \(w\in V\backslash\{t\}\) _for which G<sub>w</sub>_:=_G_+(_w,t_) _satisfies_ \(\lambda_{G_w}(s,t)=\lambda_G(s,t)+1\).

## Algebraic Primitives

We now state the algebraic tools that we use to compute determinants of low-degree polynomial matrices in (near) matrix-multiplication time. We shall use F to denote a field. Recall that F\[_Y_\] is used to denote the ring of polynomials in _Y_ with coefficients from F. Given a non-negative integer _d_, let F_<sub>d</sub>_\[_Y_\] be the subset of polynomials in F\[_Y_\] of degree at most _d_. Finally, we shall use \(\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{N\times N}\) to denote the set of \(N\times N\) matrices whose entries belong to F_<sub>d</sub>_\[_Y_\].

**Lemma 2.2.** _For any matrix_ \(M\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{N\times N}\)_, one can compute_ det(_M_) _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(dN^\omega)\) _field operations._

**Lemma 2.3** (Matrix Determinant Lemma)**.** _Let_ \(M\in\mathbb{F}_d^{N\times N}\) _be an invertible matrix and let_ \(U,V\in\mathbb{F}_d^{N\times k}\)_. Then_

\(det(M+UV^T)=det(M)\cdot det(I_k+V^TM^{-1}U).\)

Our results also employ the oracle by Brand and Saranurak \[vdBS19\] that preprocesses a matrix _H_ to efficiently answer determinant queries following a limited number of updates to _H_.

**Lemma 2.4** (\[vdBS19, Corollary of Theorem 4.1\])**.** _Let_ \(M\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{N\times N}\) _be a matrix such that_ \(det(M)\neq 0\)_. Then, there is an algorithm that preprocesses M using_ \(\widetilde{O}(dN^3)\) _operations and creates a data structure occupying O(dN_<sup>3</sup>log_N_) _space with the following guarantee: given_ \(C\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{N\times N}\) _with at most_ \(\delta\) _nonzero entries and satisfying_ \(det(M+C)\neq 0\)_, one can query_ det(_M+C_) _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(dN\delta^\omega)\) _operations._

_Moreover, if d_=0_, then the preprocessing, space and query time are_ \(O(N^\omega)\)_, O(N_<sup>2</sup>log_N_) _and_ \(O(\delta^\omega)\) _respectively._

While the above lemma assumes a non-singular base matrix, we show in Appendix that this result can be naturally extended to general, possibly singular matrices with same asymptotic complexity bounds.

We next state two determinant identities that will be used to expand determinants of products of rectangular matrices and to decompose determinants of block-structured representation matrices.

**Lemma 2.5** (Cauchy-Binet)**.** _Let A and B be two_ \(r\times m\) _matrices with_ \(m\ge r\)_. Then_

\(det(AB^T)=\sum_{S\subseteq[m]|S|=r}det(A_S)det(B_S),\)

_where the sum ranges over all_ \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{r}\) _subsets S of size r, and A<sub>S</sub>, B<sub>S</sub> denote the corresponding_ \(r\times r\) _submatrices._

**Lemma 2.6** (Generalized Laplace expansion)**.** _Let A be an_ \(n\times n\) _matrix and let its rows be partitioned into k contiguous blocks R_<sub>1</sub>_,...,R<sub>k</sub> of sizes r_<sub>1</sub>_,...,r<sub>k</sub> with_ \(\sum_ir_i=n\)_. Then_

\(det(A)=\sum_{S_1\unknown\cdots\unknown S_k=[n]|S_i|=r_i}(-1)^{\sigma(S_1,\dots,S_k)}\prod_{i=1}^kdet(A_{R_i,S_i}),\)

_where the sum is taken over all ordered partitions of the columns_ \[_n_\] _into blocks_ \(S_1\unknown\cdots\unknown S_k\) _with_ |_S<sub>i</sub>_|=_r<sub>i</sub>, and_ \((-1)^{\sigma(S_1,\dots,S_k)}\) _is the sign of the permutation that reorders_ \[_n_\] _into_ (_S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>k</sub>)._

We finally state the Schwartz-Zippel lemma which will be useful in providing high probability success bounds for our algorithms.

**Lemma 2.7** (Schwartz-Zippel lemma)**.** _Let P(x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>_,...,x<sub>N</sub>_) _be a non-zero polynomial of degree d over a finite field_ F_. If a point is selected uniformly at random from_ F_<sup>N</sup>, then the probability that P evaluates to a non-zero value is at least_ 1-_d/_|F|.

In this paper, we shall work with finite fields. Thus |F| will be _p<sup>r</sup>_, for some prime _p_ and integer \(r\ge 1\). We will be working with fields representable in _O_(log_n_) bits. This would support addition and multiplication over F in constant time in the Word-RAM model.

## Matroid Terminology

We next briefly review standard matroid terminology.

**Definition 2.8** (Matroid)**.** _A_ matroid _M_=(_E,_I) _consists of a finite ground set E and a collection_ I _of subsets of E, called_ independent sets, _satisfying three properties:_

1. \(\emptyset\in\mathcal{I}\) ;<tbc>

2. _if_ \(I\in\mathcal{I}\) _and_ \(I'\subseteq I\)_, then_ \(I'\in\mathcal{I}\) _; and_<tbc>

_3._ _if_ \(I_1,I_2\in\mathcal{I}\) _with_ |_I_<sub>1</sub>|_\<|I_<sub>2</sub>|_, there exists an element_ \(e\in I_2\backslash I_1\) _such that_ \(I_1\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal{I}\) .

**Definition 2.9** (Basis)**.** _A_ basis _of M is a maximal independent set. It is well known that all bases of M have the same cardinality, known as the_ rank _of the matroid, denoted r(M_) _(or simply r if M is clear from the context). We denote the set of all bases of M by_ B(_M)._

**Definition 2.10** (Linear Matroid)**.** _A matroid M_=(_E,_I) _on a ground set E of size m is said to be_ linear _if there exists a_ \(d\times m\) _matrix A over_ F _such that_ \(S\subseteq E\) _is independent iff the sub-matrix A<sub>S</sub> (columns of A indexed by S) has full column rank in_ F_. If the rank of M is r, we can assume without loss of generality that d=r._

Note that for any linear matroid _M_ of size _m_ and rank _r_ it is possible to produce a linear representation matrix _A_ of size \(r\times m\). Clearly, for such a representation _A_, any basis \(S\in\mathcal{B}(M)\) satisfies \(det(A_S)\neq 0\).

**Definition 2.11** (Sparse Linear Matroid)**.** _A linear matroid M is said to be c_-sparse _(or c_-column- sparse) _if there exists a representation matrix A for M over a field_ F _such that every column of A contains at most c non-zero entries. For convenience, we refer to the matrix as just_ sparse _if c=O_(1).

Matroids arising from graphs (such as graphic or partition matroids) naturally admit sparse representations, as their elements map to edges with constant-sized incidence bounds. We next define the notion of strongly base-orderable matroids.

**Definition 2.12** (Strongly base-orderable)**.** _A matroid M on E is_ strongly base-orderable _(SBO) if, for any two bases B_<sub>1</sub> _and B_<sub>2</sub> _of M, there exists a bijection_ \(\pi:B_1\rightarrow B_2\) _such that for every_ \(X\subseteq B_1\)_, both_

\((B_1\backslash X)\cup\pi(X)\text{\textit{and}}(B_2\backslash\pi(X))\cup X\)

_are bases of M._

Important families of SBO matroids include partition matroids, transversal matroids, gammoids, graphic matroids on _K_<sub>4</sub>-minor-free graphs, etc.

While packing common basis of two arbitrary matroids is an NP-Hard problem under the rank oracle model (NP-Hard even for two arbitrary linear matroids with given representation) \[BS21\], the following theorem by Davies and McDiarmid provides a nice characterisation for packing common basis in SBO matroids.

**Theorem 2.13** (Davies-McDiarmid \[DM76\])**.** _Let M_<sub>1</sub> _and M_<sub>2</sub> _be strongly base-orderable matroids on the same ground set E. Then for any_ \(S\subseteq E\)_, S can be partitioned into k common independent sets of M_<sub>1</sub> _and M_<sub>2</sub> _if and only if S can be partitioned into k independent sets of M_<sub>1</sub> _and into k independent sets of M_<sub>2</sub>.

## 3 Matroid Packing and Matroid Covering

In this section, we present an algebraic framework for addressing _matroid intersection packing_ and _matroid covering_ problems in the general sensitivity setting as well as _subset_ sensitivity setting.

### 3.1 Sensitivity Oracle for Matroid Intersection Packing

Let _M_<sub>1</sub>=(_E,_I<sub>1</sub>) and _M_<sub>2</sub>=(_E,_I<sub>2</sub>) be two linear matroids of rank _r_ defined on a common ground set _E_ of size _m_, and let \(wt:E\rightarrow[-W,W]\) be a weight function. Given an integer _k_, the _decision version_ of the _k_-packing problem asks whether there exists a subset _S_ of _E_ such that _S_ can be partitioned into _k_ pairwise disjoint common bases of _M_<sub>1</sub> as well as _M_<sub>2</sub> (observe that the partitioning of _S_ may differ in the two cases). The _weighted version_ asks for the minimum total weight of such a _k_-packing-set _S_, provided one exists. We approach this problem by analyzing the intersection of the _k_-fold unions of _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub>.

#### _k_-fold Matroid Union

Let _M_ be a linear matroid defined on a ground set _E_ of size _m_. Suppose _M_ has rank _r_ and is represented by a \(r\times m\) matrix _A_ over a finite field F. The _k_-fold union of _M_, denoted \(M^{\vee k}\), is a matroid whose independent sets are those subsets \(S\subseteq E\) that can be partitioned into _k_ disjoint sets \(S_1\unknown S_2\unknown\cdots\unknown S_k\) such that each _S<sub>i</sub>_ is an independent set in _M_. Note that the rank of \(M^{\vee k}\) may be much smaller than _kr_.

**Definition 3.1** (Randomized Union Representation)**.** _Let_ \(M^{\vee k}\) _be the k-fold union of a matroid M_=(_E,_I) _of rank r on m elements. A random matrix_ \(U\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times m}\) _is a randomized union representation of_ \(M^{\vee k}\) _if it satisfies the following two properties:_

1. _If a set_ \(S\subseteq E\) _is independent in_ \(M^{\vee k}\)_, then U<sub>S</sub> has full column rank with probability at least_ \(1-\frac{1}{(kr)^{\Omega(1)}}\).<tbc>

_2._ _If a set_ \(S\subseteq E\) _is dependent in_ \(M^{\vee k}\)_, then U<sub>S</sub> does not have full column rank (this holds deterministically)._<tbc>

The following lemma shows how to compute a randomized union representation of \(M^{\vee k}\) from a linear representation of _M_. For the sake of completeness, we provide a proof in the appendix.

**Lemma 3.2** (\[NSV94\])**.** _Let M be a linear matroid of rank r on m elements, represented by an_ \(r\times m\) _matrix A over a finite field_ F _with_ \(|\mathbb{F}|\ge poly(kr)\)_. For each_ \(i\in[k]\)_, let C<sub>i</sub> be an_ \(m\times m\) _diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are independent, uniformly random elements from_ F_. Then the_ \(rk\times m\) _matrix_

\(U:=\left(\begin{array}{ c }
AC_1 \\
AC_2 \\
\vdots \\
AC_k
\end{array}\right)\)

_is a randomized union representation of_ \(M^{\vee k}\).

**Remark 3.3** (Parallel Elements in _k_-Fold Union)**.** _Observe that it is possible that an independent set in_ \(M^{\vee k}\) _contains k identical copies of an element, i.e., the columns of A corresponding to this independent set may contain k identical columns. This is consistent with the definition of_ \(M^{\vee k}\)_, since an independent set_ \(S\subseteq E\) _in_ \(M^{\vee k}\) _is partitioned into k blocks_ \(S_1\unknown\cdots\unknown S_k\)_, each being an independent set in M; thus each such block may contain at most one copy of such an element. The representation U remains valid, as the diagonal scalings C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>k</sub> assign independent random multipliers to each (element, copy) pair._

## Intersection of two _k_-Fold Matroid Unions

Given two linear matroids _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub> of rank _r_ on a common ground set _E_, we consider the problem of identifying existence of a common basis in \(M_1^{\vee k}\) and \(M_2^{\vee k}\) of size _kr_. Let _U_<sub>1</sub> and _U_<sub>2</sub> be the \(kr\times m\) union representation matrices for \(M_1^{\vee k}\) and \(M_2^{\vee k}\), respectively, constructed using independent random diagonal matrices as given in Theorem 3.2. With each element \(e\in E\), we associate a value _x<sub>e</sub>_ drawn uniformly from a large enough finite field F. Define a diagonal matrix \(D\in\mathbb{F}[Y]^{m\times m}\) with an indeterminate _Y_ as follows:

\(D_{e,e}:=x_eY^{W+wt(e)}\text{for all}e\in E,\)

and \(D_{e,e^\prime}=0\) for \(e\neq e'\).

We next define the _Mixed Laplacian_ \(\mathcal{L}_\cap\) of size \(kr\times kr\) as:

\(\mathcal{L}_\cap:=U_1DU_2^T.\)

The following theorem extends the classical Cauchy-Binet approach for matroid intersection \[Har09, CLL14\] to the _k_-fold union setting.

**Theorem 3.4** (Enumerating Common Bases)**.** _Suppose both_ \(M_1^{\vee k}\) _and_ \(M_2^{\vee k}\) _have rank kr, and_ \(|\mathbb{F}|\ge poly(kr)\)_. Then_

\(det(\mathcal{L}_\cap)=Y^{krW}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{B}(M_1^{\vee k})\cap\mathcal{B}(M_2^{\vee k})}\alpha_S\big(\prod_{e\in S}x_e\big)Y^{\sum_{e\in S}wt(e)},\)

_where_ \(\alpha_S:=det\big((U_1)_S\big)det\big((U_2)_S\big)\) _for any common basis S is non-zero with probability_ \(1-\frac{1}{(kr)^{\Omega(1)}}\)_. Furthermore, with the same probability bound, the minimum degree of Y in_ \(det(\mathcal{L}_\cap)\) _minus krW equals the weight of a minimum-weight common basis._

_Proof._ We evaluate the determinant of the Matroid Laplacian \(\mathcal{L}_\cap=U_1DU_2^T\) using the Cauchy-Binet formula (see Theorem 2.5) and substitute \(det(D_S)=\prod_{e\in S}x_eY^{W+wt(e)}\) and \(\alpha_S\) to get:

\(det(\mathcal{L}_\cap)=det\big(U_1(DU_2^T)\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq E|S|=kr}det\big((U_1)_S\big)det\big((U_2)_S\big)det(D_S)=Y^{krW}\sum_{S\subseteq E|S|=kr}\alpha_S\big(\prod_{e\in S}x_e\big)Y^{wt(S)}.\)

By Theorem 3.2, if _S_ is dependent in either \(M_j^{\vee k}\), then (_U<sub>j</sub>)<sub>S</sub>_ does not have full column rank, and so \(\alpha_S=0\). This restricts the sum to common bases. Next, if _S_ is a common basis, then by the probabilistic claim in Theorem 3.2, each (_U<sub>j</sub>)<sub>S</sub>_ has full column rank with probability at least \(1-1/(kr)^{\Omega(1)}\), and so \(\alpha_S\neq 0\) with at least this probability.

For the final claim, let **_wt_**<sub>min</sub> denote the minimum weight of a common basis of \(M_1^{\vee k}\) and \(M_2^{\vee k}\). Then, the coefficient of \(Y^{krW+wt_\mathrm{min}}\) is \(\sum_{S^*}\alpha_{S^*}\prod_{e\in S^*}x_e\), where the sum is over minimum-weight common bases. The above is a nonzero polynomial of degree _kr_ since distinct bases contribute distinct monomials in {_x<sub>e</sub>_}, and with high probability at least one minimum-weight common basis _S_<sup>∗</sup> satisfies \(\alpha_{S^*}\neq 0\). By the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, it evaluates to a nonzero value with probability 1-_kr/_|F|. Therefore, we get that with probability \(1-\frac{1}{(kr)^{\Omega(1)}}\), isolating the smallest exponent of _Y_ in \(det(\mathcal{L}_\cap)\) and subtracting _krW_ yields **_wt_**<sub>min</sub>.

## 3.1.1 Sensitivity Oracle for Sparse Linear Matroids

We now consider the sensitivity problem for the _k_-packing problem in the setting of sparse linear matroids. To obtain _k_ disjoint common bases of two matroids _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub>, we find a common basis of full rank _kr_ in the _k_-fold union of these matroids. The main technical tool for this proceeds by analyzing the determinant of the mixed Laplacian using Theorem 3.4. In the static setting, this determinant evaluates to a non-zero polynomial with high probability if and only if a valid _k_-packing exists, and its minimum degree extracts the minimum weight of such a packing.

We formalize this in the sensitivity setting by utilizing the data structure from Theorem A.2 to handle sparse updates to the base representations of the matroids.

**Theorem 3.5.** _Let M_<sub>1</sub>=(_E,_I<sub>1</sub>) _and M_<sub>2</sub>=(_E,_I<sub>2</sub>) _be two sparse linear matroids of rank r defined on a common ground set E of size m, with a weight function_ \(wt:E\rightarrow[-W,W]\)_. Let A_<sub>1</sub> _and A_<sub>2</sub> _be their respective_ \(r\times m\) _linear representation matrices over a field_ F.

_Then, for any_ \(k\ge 1\)_, there exist sensitivity oracles that, given a set of_ \(\delta\) _updates to A_<sub>1</sub>_,A_<sub>2</sub>_, and wt, answer k-packing queries for the updated matroids_ \(M'_1\) _and_ \(M'_2\) _as follows:_

1. **_Decision Oracle:_** _Decides if a k-packing set S exists. Recall that a subset_ \(S\subseteq E,|S|=kr\) _is said to be k-packing if it can be partitioned into k common bases of_ \(M'_1\) _and_ \(M'_2\) _respectively, where the partitioning corresponding to each of the matroids may differ. This oracle requires_ \(O(k^2m+(kr)^\omega)\) _preprocessing time, O(km_+(_kr_)<sup>2</sup>log(_kr_)) _space, and answers queries in_ \(O((k^2\delta)^\omega)\) _time._<tbc>

_2._ **_Weighted Oracle:_** _Returns the exact total weight of a minimum-weight k-packing set S. This oracle requires_ \(\widetilde{O}(k^2m+W(kr)^3)\) _preprocessing time, O(km+W(kr_)<sup>3</sup>log(_kr_)) _space, and answers queries in_ \(\widetilde{O}(W\cdot kr\cdot(k^2\delta)^\omega)\) _time._

_Proof._ Let _U_<sub>1</sub> and _U_<sub>2</sub> be the \(kr\times mk\)-fold randomized union representation matrices for _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub> respectively, as obtained by Theorem 3.2. Let _D_ be the \(m\times m\) diagonal weight matrix with \(D_{e,e}=x_eY^{W+wt(e)}\), and define the \(kr\times kr\) mixed Laplacian matrix as \(\mathcal{L}_{pack}:=U_1DU_2^T\). Suppose the base representations _A_<sub>1</sub>_,A_<sub>2</sub> and the weight function undergo at most \(\delta\) changes. We first bound<tbc>

<tbc>the number of non-zero entries in the resulting additive update to the mixed Laplacian. The matrix L_<sub>pack</sub>_ can be expressed as:

\(\mathcal{L}_{pack}=\sum_{e\in E}D_{e,e}(u_1)_e(u_2)_e^T\)

where (_u_<sub>1</sub>)_<sub>e</sub>_ and (_u_<sub>2</sub>)_<sub>e</sub>_ are the _e_-th columns of _U_<sub>1</sub> and _U_<sub>2</sub>, respectively. Computing the matrix L_<sub>pack</sub>_ takes _O(k_<sup>2</sup>_m_) time, assuming that representation matrices _A_<sub>1</sub>_,A_<sub>2</sub> are provided in sparse column format (see Theorem 2.11). Note that the updates to the _e_-th column of _A_<sub>1</sub>_,A_<sub>2</sub>, or to **_wt_**(_e_) modify only the _e_-th term in the sum, and since _A_<sub>1</sub> and _A_<sub>2</sub> are column-sparse, the product \((u_1)_e(u_2)_e^T\) has at most _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) non-zero entries. Thus, for any \(\delta\) base changes, the updated Laplacian can be represented as \(\mathcal{L}'_{pack}=\mathcal{L}_{pack}+C\), where matrix _C_ has at most \(O(k^2\delta)\) non-zero entries. By Theorem 3.4, identifying the existence or computing the minimum weight of a _k_-packing set _S_ in the updated matroids reduces to evaluating the determinant of \(\mathcal{L}'_{pack}\).

To efficiently support these queries, we construct two separate oracles based on the data structure from Theorem A.2:

### Decision Oracle

We ignore the polynomial weights and work with the Laplacian L_<sub>pack</sub>|<sub>Y=1</sub>_ (where the maximum degree is _d_=0). Theorem A.2 together with the fact that _M_<sub>1</sub>_,M_<sub>2</sub> are column sparse implies that preprocessing this matrix requires \(O(k^2m+(kr)^\omega)\) time and the corresponding data structure takes _O(km_+(_kr_)<sup>2</sup>log(_kr_)) space. The additive _O(km_) term arises from the fact that storing the union representations _U_<sub>1</sub> and _U_<sub>2</sub> requires _O(km_) space. After at most \(\delta\) updates to representation matrices _A_<sub>1</sub>_,A_<sub>2</sub>, and **_wt_**, querying the determinant of the Laplacian \(\mathcal{L}'_{pack}|_{Y=1}=\mathcal{L}_{pack}|_{Y=1}+C|_{Y=1}\) requires \(O((k^2\delta)^\omega)\) query time.

### Weighted Oracle

The matrix \(\mathcal{L}_{pack}\in\mathbb{F}_{2W}[Y]^{kr\times kr}\) is a polynomial matrix where the maximum degree of _Y_ in any entry is bounded by _d_=2_W_. Theorem A.2 together with the fact that _M_<sub>1</sub>_,M_<sub>2</sub> are column sparse implies that preprocessing this matrix requires \(\widetilde{O}(k^2m+W(kr)^3)\) time and the oracle takes _O(km+W(kr_)<sup>3</sup>log(_kr_)) space. To compute the weight after any \(\delta\) updates to _A_<sub>1</sub>_,A_<sub>2</sub>_,**wt**_, we evaluate the determinant of the polynomial matrix \(\mathcal{L}'_{pack}\) and extract the coefficient of the minimum degree term of _Y_ . Querying the determinant of this updated matrix takes \(\widetilde{O}(W\cdot kr\cdot(k^2\delta)^\omega)\) time, and isolating the smallest exponent of _Y_ in \(\mathrm{det}(\mathcal{L}'_{pack})\) and subtracting _krW_ yields the exact weight of the minimum-weight _k_-packing set. This completes the proof. □

**Remark 3.6** (Cost of Parallel Updates)**.** _The query complexity in Theorem 3.5 can be refined when some of the updates correspond to changes in the multiplicity of parallel elements. Suppose the updates affect distinct elements_ \(e_1,\dots,e_\rho\) _(with_ \(\rho\le\delta\)_), where the multiplicity of e<sub>i</sub> increases or decreases by_ \(\rho_i\le k\)_, so that_ \(\sum_{i=1}^\rho\rho_i=\delta\)_. Column-sparsity of A_<sub>1</sub>_,A_<sub>2</sub> _ensures that each_ \((e_i,\rho_i)\) _contributes only O(k_<sup>2</sup>) _non-zero entries within an_ \(O(k)\times O(k)\) _submatrix of the additive update C to the packing Laplacian_ \(\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{pack}=U_1DU_2^T\)_. Aggregating over all_ \(\rho\) _affected elements, this yields query time_ \(O((k^2\rho)^\omega)\) _rather than_ \(O((k^2\delta)^\omega)\).

## 3.1.2 Subset Sensitivity Oracle for General Linear Matroids

The oracle in Theorem 3.5 handles arbitrary updates to the ground set, incurring a query cost of \(\Omega((k^2\delta)^\omega)\). We now present a complementary oracle for the _subset sensitivity model_: a _susceptible set E<sub>Q</sub>_ of size \(\sigma\) is identified at preprocessing time, and all future queries modify only elements in _E<sub>Q</sub>_. The set _E<sub>Q</sub>_ need not be a subset of _E_; we require only that the matroids _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub> admit well-defined extensions to the augmented ground set \(E_0:=E\cup E_Q\).

**Theorem 3.7.** _Let M_<sub>1</sub>=(_E,_I<sub>1</sub>) _and M_<sub>2</sub>=(_E,_I<sub>2</sub>) _be two linear matroids each of rank r on a ground set E of size m, with weight function_ \(wt:E\rightarrow[-W,W]\)_. Let E<sub>Q</sub> be a susceptible set of size_ \(\sigma\)_, and suppose M_<sub>1</sub> _and M_<sub>2</sub> _extend to linear matroids of (same) rank r on_ \(E_0:=E\cup E_Q\) _with_ \(r\times|E_0|\) _representation matrices_ \(\bar{A}_1\) _and_ \(\bar{A}_2\) _over_ F_. Then, for any_ \(k\ge 1\)_, there exist the following subset sensitivity oracles that, for any f updates confined to E<sub>Q</sub>, answer k-packing queries:_

1. **_Decision Oracle:_** _Decides if a k-packing exists. This oracle requires_ \(O(k^2(m+\sigma)+\sigma^2(kr)^{\omega-2}+(kr)^\omega)\) _preprocessing time,_ \(O(\sigma^2)\) _space, and answers queries in_ \(O(f^\omega)\) _time._<tbc>

_2._ **_Weighted Oracle:_** _Returns the exact minimum weight of a k-packing. This oracle requires_ \(\widetilde{O}(k^2(m+\sigma)+W\sigma^2(kr)^{\omega-1}+W(kr)^{\omega+1})\) _preprocessing time,_ \(\widetilde{O}(W\cdot kr\cdot\sigma^2)\) _space, and answers queries in_ \(\widetilde{O}(W\cdot kr\cdot f^\omega)\) _time._

_Proof._ Let \(\bar{U}_1,\bar{U}_2\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times|E_0|}\) be the _k_-fold union representation matrices for the extensions of _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub> to _E_<sub>0</sub>, constructed via Theorem 3.2 from \(\bar{A}_1\) and \(\bar{A}_2\). Let \(D\in\mathbb{F}_{2W}[Y]^{|E_0|\times|E_0|}\) be the diagonal weight matrix with \(D_{e,e}=x_eY^{W+wt(e)}\) for \(e\in E_0\), so that the Packing Laplacian is \(\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{pack}=\bar{U}_1D\bar{U}_2^T\). Computing L<sub>pack</sub> takes \(O(k^2(m+\sigma))\) time, since \(|E_0|=m+\sigma\) and each element contributes _O(k_<sup>2</sup>) entries to the Laplacian.

Since all queries modify only diagonal entries indexed by _E<sub>Q</sub>_, we invoke Theorem A.1 with \(A:=\bar{U}_1\), \(B:=\bar{U}_2\), the diagonal matrix _D_, and susceptible set _Q_:=_E<sub>Q</sub>_ of size \(\sigma\).

## Decision Oracle.

We apply the scalar formulation of Theorem A.1 with _d_:=0, working with L<sub>pack</sub>|<sub>_Y_=1</sub>. Substituting _r_:=_kr_ and \(\sigma=|E_Q|\) into Theorem A.1, the data structure construction takes \(O(\sigma^2(kr)^{\omega-2}+(kr)^\omega)\) time and \(O(\sigma^2)\) space. Combined with the \(O(k^2(m+\sigma))\) cost of computing L<sub>pack</sub>, the total preprocessing time is \(O(k^2(m+\sigma)+\sigma^2(kr)^{\omega-2}+(kr)^\omega)\). Each query takes \(O(f^\omega)\) time. By Theorem 3.4, the determinant is non-zero if and only if a valid _k_-packing exists.

## Weighted Oracle.

We apply the polynomial formulation of Theorem A.1 with _d_:=2_W_. Substituting _r_:=_kr_ into Theorem A.1, the data structure construction takes \(\widetilde{O}(W\sigma^2(kr)^{\omega-1}+W(kr)^{\omega+1})\) time and \(\widetilde{O}(W\cdot kr\cdot\sigma^2)\) space. Combined with the Laplacian computation, the total preprocessing time is \(\widetilde{O}(k^2(m+\sigma)+W\sigma^2(kr)^{\omega-1}+W(kr)^{\omega+1})\). Each query takes \(\widetilde{O}(W\cdot kr\cdot f^\omega)\) time. The minimum weight is extracted as the smallest exponent of _Y_ with a non-zero coefficient, minus _krW_. □

**Remark 3.8** (Comparison of Oracle Models)**.** _The general and subset sensitivity oracles for matroid packing offer complementary trade-offs:_

_The subset sensitivity oracle achieves query time independent of k, at the cost of space scaling with the susceptible set size_ \(\sigma\) _rather than the matroid rank. When_ \(\sigma\checkmark m\) _and k is large relative to f, the subset sensitivity model provides both smaller space and faster queries. When_ \(\sigma\) _is comparable to m, the general sensitivity oracle is more space-efficient._

## 3.2 Sensitivity Oracle for Matroid Covering

We next present an algebraic framework for addressing _matroid covering_.

Let _M_=(_E,_I) be a linear matroid of rank _r_ represented by an \(r\times m\) matrix _A_ over a field F. The _k-covering problem_ asks whether the entire ground set _E_ can be covered by (partitioned into) _k_ independent sets of _M_. This is equivalent to asking whether the entire ground set _E_ is an independent set in the _k_-fold union matroid \(M^{\vee k}\).

For _E_ to be an independent set in \(M^{\vee k}\), its cardinality _m_ must be at most _kr_. Let \(U\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times m}\) be the union representation matrix obtained via Theorem 3.2. The set _E_ is a _k_-covering if and only if the columns of _U_ are linearly independent. To test this, we augment _U_ into a square matrix by adding random columns.

**Lemma 3.9** (Augmenting Linear Representations)**.** _Let_ \(U\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times m}\) _be the k-fold union representation matrix for_ \(M^{\vee k}\)_. Suppose_ \(m\le kr\)_. Let_ \(\Delta=kr-m\)_, and_ \(R\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times\Delta}\) _be a random matrix whose entries are chosen independently and uniformly from a sufficiently large finite field_ F.

_Then, with high probability, the augmented square matrix_ \(U_{aug}:=[U|R]\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times kr}\) _has full rank kr if and only if the row rank of U is m, i.e., E is k-coverable._

_Proof._ We treat the entries of the random matrix _R_ as indeterminates and work over the polynomial ring F\[X\], where<tbc>

\(\mathcal{X}:=\{R_{i,j}:1\le i\le kr,1\le j\le\Delta\}.\)

<tbc>Using the block decomposition, the determinant of the \(kr\times kr\) augmented matrix _U<sub>aug</sub>_=\[_U|R_\] can be expressed as:

\(det(U_{aug})=\sum_{S\subseteq[kr]|S|=m}(-1)^{\sigma(S)}det(U_S)det(R_{S^c}),\)

where _U<sub>S</sub>_ denotes the \(m\times m\) submatrix of _U_ induced by the rows in _S_, _R<sub>S<sup>c</sup></sub>_ denotes the \(\Delta\times\Delta\) submatrix of _R_ induced by the rows in _S<sup>c</sup>_, and \(\sigma(S)\) is the corresponding sign parity.

If the row rank of _U_ is less than _m_, then every \(m\times m\) minor det(_U<sub>S</sub>_) evaluates to 0, making det(_U<sub>aug</sub>_) identically the zero polynomial.

Let us suppose the row rank of _U_ is exactly _m_. Then there exists at least one subset of rows \(S\subseteq[kr]\) such that the minor det(_U<sub>S</sub>_) is a non-zero constant in F. For each such _S_, the corresponding determinant det(_R<sub>S<sup>c</sup></sub>_) contributes distinct monomials in the variables X. Moreover, the monomials generated by one row subset _S_ cannot be cancelled out by the monomials generated by any other subset \(S'\neq S\). Thus, det(_U<sub>aug</sub>_) is a non-zero polynomial.

As entries of _R_ are chosen independently and uniformly at random from a sufficiently large finite field, by the Schwartz-Zippel lemma det(_U<sub>aug</sub>_) evaluates to a non-zero value with high probability. This proves that with high probability, the matrix _U<sub>aug</sub>_ has rank _kr_ if and only if _U_ has rank _m_. □

### 3.2.1 Sensitivity Oracle for Sparse Linear Matroids

Building on Theorem 3.9, we now present the sensitivity oracle for the _k_-covering problem.

**Theorem 3.10.** _Let_ \(k\ge 1\) _be an integer. Let M_=(_E,_I) _be a linear matroid of rank r defined on a ground set E of size_ \(m(\le kr)\)_, represented by an_ \(r\times m\) _matrix A over a field_ F_. Then, there exists a sensitivity oracle that, for any changes to M consisting of at most_ \(\delta\) _updates to A, can decide whether the entire ground set E can be covered by (partitioned into) k independent sets of the updated matroid_ \(M'\)_. This oracle requires_ \(O((kr)^\omega)\) _preprocessing time, O_((_kr_)<sup>2</sup>log(_kr_)) _space, and answers queries in_ \(O((\delta k)^\omega)\) _time._

_Proof._ Let \(U\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times m}\) be the _k_-fold union representation matrix for _M_, constructed using Theorem 3.2. Let \(\Delta=kr-m\), and let \(R\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times\Delta}\) be a matrix of independent uniformly random elements from F. We define the \(kr\times kr\) augmented matrix as _U<sub>aug</sub>_:=\[_U|R_\].

By Theorem 3.9, the set _E_ can be covered by _k_ independent sets if and only if the row rank of _U_ is _m_. With high probability, this occurs if and only if the scalar matrix _U<sub>aug</sub>_ is nonsingular.

To efficiently support queries, we apply the preprocessing algorithm from Theorem A.2 to _U<sub>aug</sub>_. This preprocessing requires \(O((kr)^\omega)\) time and computes an _O_((_kr_)<sup>2</sup>log(_kr_)) sized oracle.

Now any \(\delta\) changes to _A_ translates to exactly \(k\delta\) changes in _U_ with the random augmenting matrix _R_ completely unchanged. So, the updated augmented matrix \(U'_{aug}\) can be written as _U<sub>aug</sub>+C_, where the additive update matrix \(C\in\mathbb{F}^{kr\times kr}\) contains at most \(k\delta\) non-zero entries.

To answer a _k_-covering query for the updated matroid \(M'\), we must determine if \(det(U'_{aug})\) is nonzero. By Theorem A.2, this requires exactly \(O((\delta k)^\omega)\) time. This completes the proof. □

## 4.2 Sensitivity Oracles for (_s,t_)-Max-Flow and (_s,t_)-Min-Cut

We now turn to the special case of the general max-flow problem for a fixed source-sink pair (_s,t_). The oracle of Theorem 4.2 with _k=n_ already solves this problem, but its query time is quite high. We show that much better bounds are achievable for the case of a fixed source-sink pair through a flow-rerouting reduction that lets us use Theorem 4.2 as a black box on an auxiliary graph with capacity bound _k=O(f_).

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a directed graph with unit edge capacities and costs in \[-_W,W_\], with fixed source _s_ and sink _t_. We precompute a min-cost (_s,t_)-max-flow _h_ once, during preprocessing. For any query set _U_ of updates, we aim to answer the following: how can _h_ be _repaired_ into a valid flow on _G+U_, and by how much does its cost change.

To achieve this, we augment _G_ to a graph G by adding 2_f_ zero-cost parallel (_s,t_)-edges, and saturating the first _f_ of them in the preprocessed flow _h_ (thus, value of flow _h_ (denoted by val(_h_)) in G is equal to \(f+\lambda_G(s,t)\)). These parallel edges act as a buffer: when updates arrive, they absorb or release flow as needed, and the number of saturated parallel (_s,t_) edges in the repaired flow tells us the new max-flow value.

**Lemma 4.3.** _For any update set U of size at most f, if every_ (_s,t_)_-flow of value_ val(_h_) _in_ G+_U saturates a minimum of i parallel_ (_s,t_) _edges, then_ \(\lambda_{G+U}(s,t)=\lambda_G(s,t)+f-i\).

_Proof._ Let \(\beta:=\lambda_{G+U}(s,t)-\lambda_G(s,t)\). If \(\beta\ge 0\), \(\beta\) units of flow can be moved from the parallel edges back into _G+U_, so the new flow saturates \(i=f-\beta\) parallel edges. If \(\beta<0\), the updates cancel \(|\beta|\) units of flow in _G_, which must be redirected onto the parallel edges, giving \(i=f+|\beta|\). In both cases, \(\beta=f-i\). □

### Reducing to an All-Pairs Query

It remains to test, given a candidate value of _i_, whether _h_ can in fact be repaired in G+_U_ using exactly _i_ parallel (_s,t_) edges. We construct an auxiliary<tbc>

<tbc>multigraph \(\mathcal{G}_h^*\) from the residual graph G_<sub>h</sub>_ by adjoining a dummy source _s_<sup>∗</sup> and a dummy sink _t_<sup>∗</sup>, both initially isolated.

Given a query _U_=(_I,F_), let \(F_h:=\{e\in F:h(e)=1\}\) denote the set of deleted edges that carried flow, and for each such _e_=(_x,y_) let _e_<sup>rev</sup>=(_y,x_) denote its residual counterpart in G_<sub>h</sub>_. We define the auxiliary update set \(\mathcal{U}^*=(I^*,F^*)\) on \(\mathcal{G}_h^*\) as

\(\mathcal{U}^*:=\big(\underbrace{I\cup\{(s^*,x),(y,t^*):(x,y)\in F_h\}}_{I^*},\underbrace{(F\backslash F_h)\cup\{e^\mathrm{rev}:e\in F_h\}}_{F^*}\big).\)

That is, _I_<sup>∗</sup> inserts the edges of _I_ together with zero-cost edges incident to the dummy vertices, while _F_<sup>∗</sup> deletes the edges of _F_ that did not carry flow and the residual counterparts of those that did. Let \(\mathcal{G}^*:=\mathcal{G}_h^*+\mathcal{U}^*\); note that |U<sup>∗</sup>|=_O_(|_U_|).

**Lemma 4.4.** _Let U_=(_I,F_) _be a set of updates, and write d_:=|_F<sub>h</sub>|. The flow h in_ G _can be repaired into a valid flow_ \(h'\) _in_ G+_U if and only if the_ (_s_<sup>∗</sup>_,t_<sup>∗</sup>)_-max-flow in_ G<sup>∗</sup> _equals d. Moreover, the minimum cost of any such repaired flow satisfies_

\(c(h')=c_\mathcal{G}(h)+c_{\mathcal{G}^*}(s^*,t^*)-\sum_{e\in F_h}c(e).\)

_Proof._ Each edge \((x,y)\in F_h\) leaves _h_ with one unit of excess at _x_ and one of deficit at _y_; all other vertices remain balanced. Repairing _h_ is therefore equivalent to routing |_F<sub>h</sub>_| edge-disjoint paths in G_<sub>h</sub>_+U<sup>∗</sup> from the excess set \(X:=\{x:(x,y)\in F_h\}\) to the deficit set \(Y:=\{y:(x,y)\in F_h\}\). Since G<sup>∗</sup> adds exactly one zero-cost edge from _s_<sup>∗</sup> into each \(x\in X\) and one from each \(y\in Y\) to _t_<sup>∗</sup>, such a routing exists if and only if all _d_ edges leaving _s_<sup>∗</sup> in G<sup>∗</sup> are saturable, i.e., \(\lambda_{\mathcal{G}^*}(s^*,t^*)=d\).

We now derive the cost relation. Any min-cost (_s_<sup>∗</sup>_,t_<sup>∗</sup>)-flow _h_<sup>∗</sup> in G<sup>∗</sup> is decomposable into _d_ paths \(P_j^*=s^*\rightarrow x_j\unknown y_{\sigma(j)}\rightarrow t^*\), for some permutation \(\sigma\), and a (possibly empty) collection of negative-cost cycles \(C_1,\dots,C_\ell\) (which can appear due to insertions). The edges incident to _s_<sup>∗</sup> and _t_<sup>∗</sup> have zero cost and they cannot lie on any cycle, so \(c_{\mathcal{G}^*}(h^*)\) equals the total cost of the subpaths \(P_j:=P_j^*[x_j,y_{\sigma(j)}](1\le j\le d)\) and cycles \(C_1,\dots,C_\ell\) in G_<sub>h</sub>_. That is,

\(c_{\mathcal{G}^*}(s^*,t^*)=\sum_{j=1}^dc_{\mathcal{G}_h}(P_j)+\sum_{i=1}^\ell c_{\mathcal{G}_h}(C_i).\)

The repaired flow \(h'\) is obtained from _h_ by canceling flow along edges in _F<sub>h</sub>_ and rerouting it through the _P<sub>j</sub>_’s and _C<sub>i</sub>_’s. This removes the |_F<sub>h</sub>_| deleted-edge contributions to **_c_**(_h_) and adds the right-hand side above:

\(c(h')=c_\mathcal{G}(h)-\sum_{e\in F_h}c(e)+\sum_jc_{\mathcal{G}_h}(P_j)+\sum_ic_{\mathcal{G}_h}(C_i),\)

which yields the stated cost identity. \(\square\)

By Theorem 4.3, \(\lambda_{G+U}(s,t)=\lambda_G(s,t)+f-i\), where _i_ is the smallest number of parallel edges required to repair _h_. We define two linear matroids on the ground set _E<sub>H</sub>_.

## 5.2 Sensitivity Oracles for _k_-Disjoint Spanning Trees

We now apply our algebraic framework to the problem of finding _k_ edge-disjoint spanning trees in an undirected graph. Let _G_=(_V,E,**c**_) be an undirected graph with _n_ vertices, _m_ edges, and integer edge costs in \[-_W,W_\]. A spanning tree is a maximal acyclic subgraph of _G_, containing exactly _n_-1 edges. We can formulate the problem of finding _k_ edge-disjoint spanning trees as a matroid packing problem by utilizing the standard graphic matroid _M_<sub>graph</sub> of rank _r=n_-1.

**Lemma 5.5.** _An undirected graph G contains k edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if there exists a set_ \(S\subseteq E\) _of size k(n_-1) _that can be partitioned into k common bases of M_<sub>1</sub> _and M_<sub>2</sub>_, where we set both M_<sub>1</sub> _and M_<sub>2</sub> _to M_<sub>graph</sub>.

_Proof._ For the forward direction, suppose _G_ contains _k_ edge-disjoint spanning trees _T_<sub>1</sub>_,...,T<sub>k</sub>_. Let \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^kE(T_i)\). Because each _T<sub>i</sub>_ is a spanning tree, its edge set _E(T<sub>i</sub>_) forms a basis in _M_<sub>graph</sub>. Since the trees are edge-disjoint, the sets _E(T_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,E(T<sub>k</sub>_) are pairwise disjoint and perfectly partition _S_. Because _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub> are identical to _M_<sub>graph</sub>, each _E(T<sub>i</sub>_) is trivially a common basis of both matroids. Furthermore, the total size of _S_ is exactly \(\sum_{i=1}^k(n-1)=k(n-1)\).

For the converse, suppose there exists a set \(S\subseteq E\) of size _k(n_-1) that can be partitioned into _k_ disjoint sets _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B<sub>k</sub>_, where each _B<sub>i</sub>_ is a common basis of _M_<sub>1</sub> and _M_<sub>2</sub>. Since _M_<sub>1</sub>=_M_<sub>graph</sub>, each set _B<sub>i</sub>_ must be a basis of the graphic matroid, meaning the edges in _B<sub>i</sub>_ form a spanning tree of _G_. Because the sets _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B<sub>k</sub>_ partition _S_, they share no edges and are pairwise disjoint. Therefore, the subgraphs induced by _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B<sub>k</sub>_ constitute exactly _k_ edge-disjoint spanning trees in _G_. ▂
