## 6 Sensitivity Oracles for Matroid Parity

In this section, we study the _Matroid Parity_ (also known as _Matroid Matching_) problem, for linear matroids. The matroid parity problem was introduced by Lawler \[Law76\] as a common generalization of two fundamental combinatorial optimization problems: Matroid Intersection and Graph Matching. Although the matroid parity problem is intractable for general matroids \[JK82, Lov80\], it admits a polynomial time algorithm if the underlying matroid is linear \[Lov80\].

### 6.1 Algebraic tion and Enumeration

Let _M_ be a linear matroid of (even) rank _r_ over a field F, defined on a ground set of _m_ disjoint pairs of elements _E_={(_a_<sub>1</sub>_,b_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,(a<sub>m</sub>,b<sub>m</sub>_)}, and let \(wt:E\rightarrow[-W,W]\) be a weight function (the weights are associated with the pairs in _E_). The Linear Matroid Parity (LMP) problem asks whether there exists a selection of exactly _r/_2 pairs such that the union of all _r_ selected elements forms a basis of _M_. Such a valid selection is called a _parity basis_. The _weighted_ version asks for the minimum total weight of a parity basis, if one exists.

\begin{tabular}{ccccc}
_Oracle_ & _Prep._ & _Space_ & _Query_ & _Output_ \\
_Decision_ & \(O((kn)^\omega)\) & _O_((_kn_)<sup>2</sup>log_n_) & _O_((_kf_)<sup>\(\omega\)</sup>) & _Whether G+U partitions into k forests_ \\
\end{tabular}

Let \(A,B\in\mathbb{F}^{r\times m}\) be the representation matrices where the _i_-th column of _A_ corresponds to _a<sub>i</sub>_ and the _i_-th column of _B_ corresponds to _b<sub>i</sub>_. Let \(D\in\mathbb{F}_{2W}[Y]^{m\times m}\) be a diagonal matrix with _D<sub>i,i</sub>=x<sub>i</sub>Y_<sup>_W+wt(i_)</sup>, where _x<sub>i</sub>_ are independent uniformly random variables.

We define the \(r\times r\) skew-symmetric LMP matrix as:<tbc>

\(\mathcal{M}_{LMP}:=ADB^T-BDA^T\)

<tbc>**Theorem 6.1** (Enumerating Parity Bases \[Lov80, CGM92\])**.** _If the linear matroid M contains at least one parity basis, then the determinant of_ M_<sub>LMP</sub> enumerates the parity bases of M. Specifically,_

\(\mathrm{det}(\mathcal{M}_{LMP})=Y^{rW}\left(\sum_{S\subseteq[m]|S|=r/2}\mathrm{det}(M_S)\big(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\big)Y^{wt(S)}\right)^2\)

_where M<sub>S</sub> is the_ \(r\times r\) _submatrix formed by interleaving the columns a<sub>i</sub> and b<sub>i</sub> for all_ \(i\in S\)_. Furthermore, with high probability, the minimum degree of Y in_ det(M_<sub>LMP</sub>_) _minus rW equals exactly twice the weight of the minimum-weight parity basis._

_Proof._ Because M_<sub>LMP</sub>_ is a skew-symmetric matrix of even dimension _r_, its determinant is the square of a polynomial known as its Pfaffian, i.e., det(M_<sub>LMP</sub>_)=Pf(M_<sub>LMP</sub>_)<sup>2</sup>.

The Pfaffian of the matrix \(\sum_{i=1}^mx_iY^{W+wt(i)}(a_ib_i^T-b_ia_i^T)\) can be explicitly expanded as the sum of the determinants of all \(r\times r\) minors generated by subsets of size _r/_2. Specifically,

\(\mathrm{Pf}(\mathcal{M}_{LMP})=\sum_{S\subseteq[m]|S|=r/2}\mathrm{det}(M_S)\prod_{i\in S}\left(x_iY^{W+wt(a_i,b_i)}\right)\)

where _M<sub>S</sub>_ is the \(r\times r\) matrix whose columns are exactly the pairs {_a<sub>i</sub>,b<sub>i</sub>_} for \(i\in S\).

Observe that \(\mathrm{det}(M_S)\neq 0\) if and only if the columns of _M<sub>S</sub>_ are linearly independent over F. Because _M<sub>S</sub>_ contains exactly _r_ columns corresponding to _r/_2 pairs, this condition holds if and only if _S_ is a valid parity basis. Factoring out the base weight _W_ from the exponent yields:

\(\mathrm{Pf}(\mathcal{M}_{LMP})=Y^\frac{r}{2}W\sum_{S\text{is a parity basis}}\pm\mathrm{det}(M_S)\big(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\big)Y^{wt(S)}\)

Squaring the Pfaffian to obtain the determinant directly produces the formula stated in the theorem.

Let _S_<sup>∗</sup> be an optimal basis. Then the coefficient of \(Y^\frac{r}{2}W+wt(S^*)\) in Pf(M_<sub>LMP</sub>_) is a polynomial of degree _r/_2 in the variables _x<sub>i</sub>_; it is not identically zero since the monomials \(\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) of distinct minimum-weight parity bases _S_ are distinct. By the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, its evaluation at independent uniform _x<sub>i</sub>_ from a field of size \(\Omega(\text{poly}(m))\) is nonzero with high probability. Since the Pfaffian is squared, the term corresponding to optimal basis contributes a _Y_ -exponent of \(2(\frac{r}{2}W+wt(S^*))=rW+2wt(S^*)\). Therefore, isolating the smallest exponent of _Y_ in det(M_<sub>LMP</sub>_) and subtracting _rW_ yields exactly 2_wt(S_<sup>∗</sup>). □

## 7 \(\alpha\)-Factors and Matchings

Let _G_=(_V,E,c_) be an undirected graph with _n_ vertices and _m_ edges, where edge costs are integers in the range \[-_W,W_\]. Let \(\alpha:V\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^+\) be a function assigning a degree bound to each vertex in _V_ . Following the terminology of \[GS21b\], we define a (perfect) \(\alpha\)**-factor** as a subgraph _H_ of _G_ such that every vertex \(v\in V\) has degree exactly \(\alpha(v)\) in _H_. <sup>3</sup>

For convenience, we only consider the (perfect) \(\alpha\)-factor and refer to it throughout as just \(\alpha\)-factor. The _minimum-cost_ \(\alpha\)-factor is the \(\alpha\)-factor with minimum total edge cost, if it exists. Throughout this section, we refer to the set of edges incident to a vertex _v_ in graph _G_ as \(\delta_G(v)\). We omit the subscript _G_ if the graph _G_ is clear from the context.

### 7.1 \(\alpha\)-Factors as Linear Matroid Parity

In this subsection, we study the _k-bounded_ \(\alpha\)_-factor problem_, where we assume that the maximum degree constraint is bounded by a parameter _k_, i.e., \(max_{v\in V}\alpha(v)\le k\). The _k-bounded_ \(\alpha\)_-factor problem_ can be formulated as a linear matroid parity problem over a _k_-sparse linear matroid _M_ having _m_ disjoint pairs of elements. Let \(N=\sum_{v\in V}\alpha(v)\) denote the sum of all degree constraints. We assume that \(N\le 2m\) and is even, otherwise an \(\alpha\)-factor does not exist.

Furthermore, we assume that the vertex set _V_ has some fixed total ordering, i.e., for any two vertices \(a,b\in V\) , either _a\<b_ or _a\>b_. Since the graph is undirected, we assume that every edge is written as an ordered pair according to the total ordering over _V_ , i.e., an edge _e_ in _G_ is written as (_a,b_), where _a\<b_, and (_b,a_) otherwise.

Define V as a set where each vertex \(v\in V\) has \(\alpha(v)\) distinct copies, and \(v_j(j\in[\alpha(v)])\) refers to the _j<sup>th</sup>_ copy of vertex _v_.

Now, consider the following matrix representation matrix _A_ for a matroid _M_: _A_ is a \(N\times 2m\) polynomial matrix over the variables \(\{x_{u_k,e}\}_{u_k\in\mathcal{V},e\in\delta(u)}\) whose rows are indexed by V and the column<tbc>

<sup>3</sup>Note that our results carry over to (maximum) \(\alpha\)-factor as well. The (maximum) \(\alpha\)-factor considers \(\alpha(v)\) as an upper bound on the desired degree of _v_ and the objective is to maximise the number of edges picked. We provide its details in the appendix.

pairs by _E_. For _e_=(_u,v_), the two columns corresponding to _e_ are (_e<sub>u</sub>,e<sub>v</sub>_) respectively. For every edge \(e=(u,v)\in E\), set the following entries in _A_:

\(A[u_k,e_u]=x_{u_k,e};A[v_l,e_v]=x_{v_l,e}\forall k\in[\alpha(u)],l\in[\alpha(v)].\)

Rest of the entries are set to 0. It can be seen that there are no repeated non-zero entries in _A_. Now, we show the following:

**Lemma 7.1.** _A graph G contains an_ \(\alpha\)_-factor if and only if the linear matroid M represented by A admits a parity base. Furthermore, there is a bijection between the_ \(\alpha\)_-factors of G and the parity bases of M._

_Proof._ We first prove the forward direction. Let \(H\subseteq E\) be an \(\alpha\)-factor of _G_. It can be seen that |_H_|=_N/_2 and hence, _H_ induces an \(N\times N\) submatrix _A_\[_H_\], formed by selecting the column pairs of _A_ corresponding to _H_. Since \(|\delta_H(v)|=\alpha(v)\) for all \(v\in V\) , we can define a perfect matching \(\pi\) between the set V and the columns of _H_ by mapping each copy \(v_j\in\mathcal{V}\) to a unique column _e<sub>v</sub>_ for some \(e\in H\cap\delta_H(v)\). Since each indeterminate appears exactly once in the entire matrix _A_, the monomial \(\prod_{v_j\in\mathcal{V}}A_{v_j,\pi(v_j)}\) in the Leibniz expansion of det(_A_\[_H_\]) does not get cancelled. Thus, \(det(A[H])\neq 0\), meaning the pairs corresponding to _H_ form a parity base.

For the other direction, assume there exists a parity base of _M_ corresponding to the edge set \(H\subseteq E\). Note that since rank(_M_)=_N_, we have that |_H_|=_N/_2. We now show by contradiction that for all \(v\in V\) , \(|\delta_H(v)|=\alpha(v)\). Suppose this is not true. Then, there exists a vertex \(w\in V\) such that \(|\delta_H(w)|\neq\alpha(w)\). Since |_H_|=_N/_2 and \(\sum_{v\in V}\alpha(v)=N\), we can assume without loss of generality that \(|\delta_H(w)|>\alpha(w)\). Define the set _C_ as the collection of columns of _A_ indexed by the set of edges \(\{e_w|e\in\delta_H(w)\}\). Since \(|\delta_H(w)|>\alpha(w)\), we have that \(|C|>\alpha(w)\). By the definition of _A_, there exist at most \(\alpha(w)\) rows (corresponding to the copies \(\{w_1,w_2,\dots,w_{\alpha(w)}\}\)) that have non-zero entries for the column vectors in _C_. Hence, the set of columns in _C_ can span a subspace of rank at most \(\alpha(w)\). Since \(|C|>\alpha(w)\), the columns in _C_ are linearly dependent. This implies _A_\[_H_\] is singular, and therefore the pairs corresponding to _H_ do not form a parity basis, which is a contradiction. □

Since the edges of _G_ correspond to the pairs in _M_, the following corollary of Theorem 7.1 is immediate in the weighted setting:

**Corollary 7.2.** _The cost of the minimum cost_ \(\alpha\)_-factor of G is equal to the weight of minimum- weight parity basis of M, if they exist._

(Selecting this edge in a \(\beta\)-factor of _H_ implies _e_ is _dropped_ from \(M'\)).<tbc>

• **Layer 2 (add layer):** Make another copy _V_<sub>2</sub> of the vertex set _V_ , such that for any vertex \(v\in V\) , _v_<sub>2</sub> denotes its copy in the set _V_<sub>2</sub>. Recall that the \((f+k)^\omega\) query time in Theorem 8.6 is due to the fact that a query toggles _f+k_ diagonal entries: _f_ for the edge updates and _k_ for activating the parallel (_z,s_) query edges. ## 8.3 Subset Sensitivity for Matroid Parity

Recall from Section 6 that enumerating or finding the minimum-weight parity basis of a linear matroid of rank _r_ with _m_ pairs reduces to maintaining the determinant (or Pfaffian) of the \(r\times r\) skew-symmetric Linear Matroid Parity (LMP) matrix:

\(\mathcal{M}_{LMP}:=ADB^T-BDA^T,\)

where \(A,B\in\mathbb{F}^{r\times m}\) represent the static coordinate vectors of the pairs, and \(D\in\mathbb{F}(x)[Y]^{m\times m}\) is the diagonal matrix encoding pair weights and formal variables.

To maintain det(M_<sub>LMP</sub>_) in the sensitivity setting using our framework (Theorem A.1), we fac torize it into the standard form \(\hat{U}D_{ext}\hat{V}^T\). We define two augmented representation matrices:<tbc>

\(\hat{U}:=[A|B]\in\mathbb{F}^{r\times 2m}\text{and}\hat{V}:=[B|-A]\in\mathbb{F}^{r\times 2m}.\)

<tbc>Let _D<sub>ext</sub>_ be the \(2m\times 2m\) block-diagonal matrix constructed by duplicating _D_:<tbc>

\(D_{ext}:=\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
D & 0 \\
0 & D
\end{array}\right).\)

<tbc>The _Parity Laplacian_ is defined as follows and is equivalent to the LMP matrix:

\(\mathcal{L}_{parity}:=\hat{U}D_{ext}\hat{V}^T=ADB^T-BDA^T=\mathcal{M}_{LMP}.\)

This block-matrix factorization allows us to directly apply our subset sensitivity determinant data structures.

Suppose the representations of the pairs or their weights undergo an update set _U_ of size _f_. An update to pair _i_ modifies exactly two diagonal entries in _D<sub>ext</sub>_ (at indices _i_ and _i+m_). Therefore, applying _f_ pair updates translates to modifying at most 2_f_ diagonal entries in _D<sub>ext</sub>_.

(a) Since there is at most one (_s,t_)-path, the value of the 1-bounded (_s,t_)-maximum flow (equivalently, the (_s,t_)-minimum cut) value in _G+U_ is 1 if _M_\[_i,j_\]=1 and 0 otherwise.<tbc>

As discussed previously, (_s,t_)-min-cut in _G+U_ is 1 if and only if _M_\[_i,j_\]=1. Hence the value of global directed minimum cut in _G+U_ equals _M_\[_i,j_\].<tbc>

(c) From the above discussions, _s_-min-cut in _G+U_ has value exactly _M_\[_i,j_\]. Moreover, an _s_-rooted spanning arborescence exists if and only if every vertex is reachable from _s_, which holds exactly when the edge (_x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>_) is present, that is, when _M_\[_i,j_\]=1.<tbc>

Thus, each update reveals the corresponding matrix entry _M_\[_i,j_\]. Since correctly answering all _p_<sup>2</sup> queries uniquely determines _M_ and \(p=\Theta(min\{\sigma,n\})\), any subset sensitivity oracle requires \(\Omega(p^2)=\Omega\left(min\{\sigma^2,n^2\}\right)\) bits of space. □

We next present our lower bound result for colorful spanning trees.

**Theorem 9.2** (Colorful Spanning Trees)**.** _Let_ \(n,\sigma\) _be positive integers with_ \(4\le\sigma\le n(n-1)\)_. There exists an n-vertex edge-colored graph carrying a base spanning tree T_<sup>∗</sup> _and a susceptible set E<sub>Q</sub> of size_ \(\Theta(\sigma)\) _such that any subset sensitivity oracle for colorful spanning tree requires_ \(\Omega(min(\sigma^2,n^2))\) _bits of space under f_=2 _updates._

_Proof._ Set \(p=min(\lfloor\sigma/4\rfloor,\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor)\ge 1\), which ensures that \(2p+2\le n\) and \(p+1\le\sigma\). Let \(M\in\{0,1\}^{p\times p}\) be an arbitrary boolean matrix.

We construct an undirected graph _G_=(_V,E_) on exactly _n_ vertices. First, we build the core subgraph on 2_p_+2 vertices defined by \(V_\mathrm{core}=\{s,t\}\cup X\cup Y\), where _X_={_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>p</sub>_} and _Y_={_y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>p</sub>_}. The remaining _n_-(2_p_+2) vertices are added as dummy vertices to satisfy the vertex count. The edge set and color assignments for the core graph are defined as follows:

1. For each \(k\in[p]\), add the edge (_s,x<sub>k</sub>_) with color _k_. These _p_ edges have distinct colors 1_,...,p_.<tbc>

2. For each \(k\in[p]\), add the edge (_t,y<sub>k</sub>_) with color _p+k_. These _p_ edges have distinct colors _p_+1_,...,_2_p_.<tbc>

3. Add the edge (_s,t_) with color 2_p_+1.<tbc>

4. For each \((i,j)\in[p]\times[p]\) with _M_\[_i,j_\]=1, add the edge (_x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>_) with color _i_.

To ensure the entire graph is connected, add edges between the _n_-(2_p_+2) dummy vertices and _s_ using _n_-(2_p_+2) new, distinct colors. The total number of colors is exactly _n_-1. Define the susceptible set as \(E_Q=\{t\}\times(X\cup Y)\) (note \(|E_Q|=O(\sigma)\)).

Consider a target pair \((i,j)\in[p]\times[p]\). The _f_=2 update query _U_ consists of:

• Deletion of the edge (_y<sub>j</sub>,t_) of color _p+j_.<tbc>

• Insertion of a new edge (_x<sub>i</sub>,t_) of color _p+j_.

Let _G+U_ be the updated graph. To form a valid colorful spanning tree in _G+U_, exactly one edge from each of the _n_-1 color classes must be selected. We argue below that _G+U_ has a colorful spanning tree if and only if _M_\[_i,j_\]=1.

If _M_\[_i,j_\]=1, then the following is a colorful spanning tree of _G+U_: all edges incident to dummy vertices, edge (_s,t_), edges (_t,y<sub>k</sub>_) for \(k\neq j\), edges (_s,x<sub>r</sub>_) for \(r\neq i\), the inserted edge (_t,x<sub>i</sub>_) of color _p+j_, and edge (_x<sub>i</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>_) of color _i_. It is spanning, acyclic, and uses each color exactly once.

Now let _T_ be a colorful spanning tree of _G+U_. Since _T_ contains one edge per color, it contains all edges incident to dummy vertices, edge (_s,t_), edge (_t,y<sub>k</sub>_) for \(k\neq j\), and the inserted edge (_t,x<sub>i</sub>_) (the unique edge of color _p+j_ after the update). The vertex _y<sub>j</sub>_ is incident only to matrix edges, so _T_ must contain one or more edge of the form (_x<sub>a</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>_), where \(a\in[p]\). Let A be collection of indices \(a\in[p]\) such that (_x<sub>a</sub>,y<sub>j</sub>_) is an edge in _T_. If \(i\in\mathcal{A}\), then we have proved _M_\[_i,j_\]=1. If \(i\notin\mathcal{A}\), then the component of _y<sub>j</sub>_ in _T_ only consists of _y<sub>j</sub>_ together with degree-one vertices from _X_\\{_x<sub>i</sub>_} and cannot contain _t_. Indeed, each \(x_a\in X\) must have exactly one edge of color _a_ incident to it in _T_. This contradicts connectivity of _T_, and proves that a colorful spanning tree cannot exist if _M_\[_i,j_\]=0.

For each \((i,j)\in[p]^2\), the oracle’s answer uniquely determines the entry _M_\[_i,j_\]. The oracle must therefore distinguish between 2<sup>_p_<sup>2</sup></sup> configurations, establishing a space lower bound of \(p^2=\Omega(min(\sigma^2,n^2))\) bits. □

### A.1 Subset Sensitivity Oracle for Matrix Determinant

**Lemma A.1.** _Let_ \(A,B\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{r\times m}\) (\(r\le m\)), \(D\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{m\times m}\) _be a diagonal matrix and let L=ADB<sup>T</sup>. Let_ \(Q\subseteq[m]\) _be a designated_ susceptible set _of size_ \(\sigma\)_, identified at preprocessing time, such that all future queries modify only diagonal entries of D indexed by Q._

_Then there is an algorithm that preprocesses A, B, and D to construct a data structure such that, given a diagonal matrix_ \(D'\) _differing from D in at most f positions (all within Q), computes_ \(\mathrm{det}(AD'B^T)\) _with the following complexity bounds:_

1. **_Scalar (d_=0):** _If the matrices A,B have entries in_ F_, then the preprocessing time is_ \(O(\sigma^2r^{\omega-2}+r^\omega)\)_, the space requirement is_ \(O(\sigma^2)\)_, and the query time is_ \(O(f^\omega)\).<tbc>

_2._ **_Polynomial (_**\(d\ge 1\)**_):_** _If the matrices have entries in_ F_<sub>d</sub>_\[_Y_\]_, then the preprocessing time is_ \(\widetilde{O}(d\sigma^2r^{\omega-1}+dr^{\omega+1})\)_, the space requirement is_ \(\widetilde{O}(dr\sigma^2)\)_, and the query time is_ \(\widetilde{O}(drf^\omega)\).

_Proof._ Let \(A,B\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{r\times m}\) with \(r\le m\), and let \(D\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{m\times m}\). Let \(Q\subseteq[m]\) be the given _susceptible set_ of size \(\sigma\). Let \(L=ADB^T\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{r\times r}\). For a query \(D'\) that differs from _D_ on a set \(S\subseteq Q\) with \(|S|\le f\), let \(\Delta_S\) be the \(f\times f\) diagonal matrix with diagonal entries \(D'_{i_ji_j}-D_{i_ji_j}\) for \(i_j\in S\), and let _A<sub>S</sub>,B<sub>S</sub>_ be the submatrices of _A,B_ with columns indexed by _S_. The updated matrix is:<tbc>

\(L'=AD'B^T=L+A_S\Delta_SB_S^T.\)

<tbc>Let \(\delta=r-\mathrm{rank}(L)\ge 0\). Since \(\mathrm{rank}(A_S\Delta_SB_S^T)\le f\), we have:

\(\mathrm{rank}(L')\le(r-\delta)+f.\)

If \(\delta>f\), then \(\mathrm{rank}(L')<r\) for all valid queries, so \(\mathrm{det}(L')=0\) identically. In this case, we can answer every query in _O_(1) time and we are done. Thus, we assume \(\delta\le f\).

Take random matrices \(U,V\in\mathbb{F}_d^{r\times\delta}\) and let _L_<sub>pad</sub>=_L+UV<sup>T</sup>_. Since the rank deficiency of _L_ is exactly \(\delta\), there exist _U,V_ for which _L_<sub>pad</sub> is nonsingular. By the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, with high probability a random choice of _U,V_ yields \(\mathrm{det}(L_\mathrm{pad})\neq 0\), allowing us to assume _L_<sub>pad</sub> is invertible. (Note that we assume the field F is sufficiently large, in particular of size poly(_r_), which ensures that a random choice succeeds with high probability directly over F).

For any query, we can rewrite \(L'\) as:<tbc>

\(L'=L_\mathrm{pad}+\left(A_SU\right)\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\Delta_S & 0 \\
0 & -I_\delta
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ c }
B_S^T \\
V^T
\end{array}\right).\)

Let \(X=\left(A_S|U\right)\), \(Y=\left(B_S|V\right)\), and \(M_S=\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\Delta_S & 0 \\
0 & -I_\delta
\end{array}\right)\). Applying the Matrix Determinant lemma to the invertible matrix _L_<sub>pad</sub> yields:

\(det(L')=det(L_\mathrm{pad})det\big(I_{f+\delta}+M_SY^TL_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}X\big).\) (2)

### Preprocessing.

We compute _L_, its rank, and \(\delta\). If \(\delta>f\), we store a flag to return 0 for all queries. Otherwise, we sample _U,V_ until \(det(L_\mathrm{pad})\neq 0\), then compute and store det(_L_<sub>pad</sub>).

Because all queries are restricted to the susceptible set _Q_ of size \(\sigma\), the matrix \(Y^TL_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}X\) will always be a principal submatrix of a larger precomputed matrix restricted to _Q_ and the pad. We construct and store this \((\sigma+\delta)\times(\sigma+\delta)\) matrix:

\(W_Q:=\left(B_Q|V\right)^TL_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}\left(A_Q|U\right).\)

Note that since \(\delta\le f\le\sigma\), the dimensions of _W<sub>Q</sub>_ are \(O(\sigma\times\sigma)\).

• **For** _d_=0**:** Inverting _L_<sub>pad</sub> costs \(O(r^\omega)\) operations. Multiplying the \(r\times r\) matrix \(L_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}\) by the \(r\times(\sigma+\delta)\) matrix (_A<sub>Q</sub>|U_) requires \(O(\sigma r^{\omega-1}+r^\omega)\) time using rectangular matrix multiplication. Multiplying (_B<sub>Q</sub>|V)<sup>T</sup>_ by the result takes \(O(\sigma^2r^{\omega-2}+r^\omega)\) time. Thus, total preprocessing is \(O(\sigma^2r^{\omega-2}+r^\omega)\), and storing _W<sub>Q</sub>_ requires \(O(\sigma^2)\) space.<tbc>

• **For** \(d\ge 1\)**:** _L_<sub>pad</sub> is an \(r\times r\) matrix with entries of degree _d_. Thus, \(L_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}\) has entries that are rational functions of degree _O(dr_). From \[Sto15\], computing \(L_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}\) costs \(\widetilde{O}(dr^3)\) operations. By the same rectangular multiplication bounds scaled for polynomials, computing _W<sub>Q</sub>_ requires \(\widetilde{O}(d\sigma^2r^{\omega-1}+dr^{\omega+1})\) time. Storing the \(O(\sigma\times\sigma)\) matrix _W<sub>Q</sub>_ requires \(\widetilde{O}(dr\sigma^2)\) space.

### Query.

If we stored \(\delta>f\), we immediately answer 0. Otherwise, let _I<sub>S</sub>_ be the index set corresponding to the queried columns _S_ alongside the \(\delta\) pad indices. The required \((f+\delta)\times(f+\delta)\) matrix \(Y^TL_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}X\) is exactly the submatrix (_W<sub>Q</sub>)<sub>I<sub>S</sub>,I<sub>S</sub></sub>_.

We extract (_W<sub>Q</sub>)<sub>I<sub>S</sub>,I<sub>S</sub></sub>_, multiply it by _M<sub>S</sub>_, add the identity matrix \(I_{f+\delta}\), and compute the determinant of the resulting \((f+\delta)\times(f+\delta)\) matrix as per Equation (2).

• **For** _d_=0**:** Since \(f+\delta\le 2f\), evaluating this determinant costs \(O(f^\omega)\) field operations.<tbc>

• **For** \(d\ge 1\)**:** The entries of (_W<sub>Q</sub>)<sub>I<sub>S</sub>,I<sub>S</sub></sub>_ have degree _O(dr_), so computing the determinant costs \(\widetilde{O}(drf^\omega)\) field operations. Multiplying the result by the precomputed scalar det(_L_<sub>pad</sub>) completes the evaluation.

This proves the claim. \(\square\)

## A.2 Extension of Theorem 2.4 to General matrices

**Lemma A.2.** _Let_ \(M\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{N\times N}\) _be a matrix (possibly singular). Let_ \(Q\subseteq[N]\) _be a designated_ susceptible set _of size_ \(\sigma\)_, identified at preprocessing time, such that all future queries add a modification matrix_ \(C\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{N\times N}\) _whose non-zero entries are entirely confined to_ \(Q\times Q\)_. Then, there is a randomized algorithm that preprocesses M using_ \(\widetilde{O}(dN^3)\) _operations to create a data structure occupying_ \(\widetilde{O}(dN\sigma^2)\) _space with the following guarantee: given C with at most_ \(\delta_C\) _nonzero entries, one can query_ det(_M+C_) _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(dN\delta_C^\omega)\) _operations._

_Moreover, if d_=0_, then the preprocessing time, space, and query time are_ \(O(N^\omega)\), \(O(\sigma^2)\)_, and_ \(O(\delta_C^\omega)\) _respectively._

_Proof._ Let \(\delta=N-rank(M)\ge 0\) be the rank deficiency of the base matrix _M_. The modification matrix _C_ has at most \(\delta_C\) nonzero entries, meaning \(rank(C)\le\delta_C\). Therefore, the rank of the updated matrix \(M'=M+C\) is bounded by:

\(rank(M')\le(N-\delta)+\delta_C.\)

If \(\delta>\delta_C\), then \(rank(M')<N\) for all possible queries, implying det(_M+C_)=0 identically. In this scenario, the algorithm flags this condition during preprocessing and answers all queries with 0 in _O_(1) time. Thus, we assume henceforth that \(\delta\le\delta_C\).

We sample random matrices \(U,V\in\mathbb{F}_d^{N\times\delta}\). Since the rank deficiency of _M_ is exactly \(\delta\), a generic rank-\(\delta\) correction makes the matrix nonsingular. By the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, assuming the field F_<sub>d</sub>_ is of size poly(_N_), a random choice of _U,V_ ensures that _M_<sub>pad</sub>=_M+UV<sup>T</sup>_ is invertible with high probability.

Since the matrix _C_ contains at most \(\delta_C\) nonzero entries, all located within \(Q\times Q\), we can explicitly factor it as a low-rank product using only indices from _Q_. Let \(k\le\delta_C\) be the exact number of nonzero entries in _C_, located at coordinates (_i_<sub>1</sub>_,j_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,(i<sub>k</sub>,j<sub>k</sub>_) where \(i_m,j_m\in Q\). We decompose _C_ as \(C=U_C\Delta_CV_C^T\), where \(\Delta_C\in\mathbb{F}_d[Y]^{k\times k}\) is a diagonal matrix with its _m_-th diagonal entry being _C<sub>i<sub>m</sub>,j<sub>m</sub></sub>_. The matrices \(U_C,V_C\in\mathbb{F}_d^{N\times k}\) are constructed from the standard basis vectors of \(\mathbb{F}_d^N\): the _m_-th column of _U<sub>C</sub>_ is _e<sub>i<sub>m</sub></sub>_, and the _m_-th column of _V<sub>C</sub>_ is _e<sub>j<sub>m</sub></sub>_.

We can now express the query matrix \(M'\) by introducing and immediately subtracting the numeric pad:<tbc>

\(M'=M+C=M_\mathrm{pad}+C-UV^T=M_\mathrm{pad}+\left(U_CU\right)\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\Delta_C & 0 \\
0 & -I_\delta
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ c }
V_C^T \\
V^T
\end{array}\right).\)

<tbc>Let \(X=\left(U_CU\right)\), \(Y=\left(V_CV\right)\), and \(\Sigma=\left(\begin{array}{ c c }
\Delta_C & 0 \\
0 & -I_\delta
\end{array}\right)\). Applying the Matrix Determinant lemma to the invertible matrix _M_<sub>pad</sub> yields:

\(det(M+C)=det(M_\mathrm{pad})det\left(I_{k+\delta}+\Sigma Y^TM_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}X\right).\) (3)

## Preprocessing.

We compute the rank of _M_ and determine \(\delta\). If \(\delta>\delta_C\), we store a short-circuit flag. Otherwise, we sample \(U,V\) until \(det(M_\mathrm{pad})\neq 0\). We then compute det(_M_<sub>pad</sub>) and the complete inverse matrix \(M_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}\).

Because all queries restrict the non-zero entries of _C_ to the susceptible set _Q_ of size \(\sigma\), the selection matrices _U<sub>C</sub>_ and _V<sub>C</sub>_ only ever sample rows and columns from _Q_. Thus, the inner matrix \(Y^TM_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}X\) will always be a principal submatrix of a larger precomputed matrix restricted to _Q_ and the pad. We construct and store this \((\sigma+\delta)\times(\sigma+\delta)\) matrix:

\(W_Q:=\left(I_{N,Q}V\right)^TM_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}\left(I_{N,Q}U\right),\)

where _I<sub>N,Q</sub>_ represents the \(N\times\sigma\) submatrix of the identity matrix _I<sub>N</sub>_ consisting of the columns indexed by _Q_. Note that since \(\delta\le\delta_C\le\sigma\), the dimensions of _W<sub>Q</sub>_ are \(O(\sigma\times\sigma)\).

• **For** _d_=0**:** Computing \(M_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}\) costs \(O(N^\omega)\) arithmetic operations. Extracting _W<sub>Q</sub>_ and storing it requires \(O(\sigma^2)\) space.<tbc>

• **For** \(d\ge 1\)**:** The entries of _M_<sub>pad</sub> have degree _d_, meaning the entries of \(M_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}\) are rational func tions of degree _O(dN_). From \[Sto15\] (Corollary 6.12), computing this inverse costs \(\widetilde{O}(dN^3)\) operations. Storing the \(O(\sigma)\times O(\sigma)\) matrix _W<sub>Q</sub>_ requires \(\widetilde{O}(dN\sigma^2)\) space.<tbc>

### Query.

Given a modification matrix _C_, if the short-circuit flag \(\delta>\delta_C\) is active, we return 0. Otherwise, the query algorithm identifies the \(k\le\delta_C\) coordinates of the nonzero entries to form the standard basis selection matrices _U<sub>C</sub>_ and _V<sub>C</sub>_.

To form the inner matrix \(Y^TM_\mathrm{pad}^{-1}X\), we simply extract the relevant rows and columns from our precomputed matrix _W<sub>Q</sub>_. Because _U<sub>C</sub>_ and _V<sub>C</sub>_ map directly to indices within _Q_, this amounts to an \(O(\delta_C)\times O(\delta_C)\) submatrix lookup, alongside the static _U_ and _V_ blocks. Since \(\delta\le\delta_C\), the total dimension of this inner matrix is at most \(2\delta_C\times 2\delta_C\).

We multiply this submatrix by \(\Sigma\), add \(I_{k+\delta}\), and evaluate its determinant.

• **For** _d_=0**:** Computing the determinant of this \(O(\delta_C)\times O(\delta_C)\) scalar matrix costs \(O(\delta_C^\omega)\) field operations.<tbc>

• **For** \(d\ge 1\)**:** The entries extracted from _W<sub>Q</sub>_ have rational degree _O(dN_). Computing the determinant of an \(O(\delta_C)\times O(\delta_C)\) matrix with entries of degree _O(dN_) takes \(\widetilde{O}(dN\delta_C^\omega)\) operations.

Multiplying this final determinant by the precomputed scalar det(_M_<sub>pad</sub>) completes the query procedure. \(\square\)

## A.3 Proof of Theorem 3.2

_Proof._ We treat the diagonal entries \(\{c_{i,e}:i\in[k],e\in E\}\) of the matrices _C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>k</sub>_ as formal variables and work over the polynomial ring F\[{_c<sub>i,e</sub>_}\].

We first show that \(S\subseteq E\) is independent in \(M^{\vee k}\) if and only if the submatrix _U<sub>S</sub>_ has full column rank over the polynomial ring (i.e., some maximal minor of _U<sub>S</sub>_ is a non-zero polynomial).

Fix \(S\subseteq E\) with |_S_|=_s_. Suppose _S_ is independent in \(M^{\vee k}\). By definition, there is a partition \(S=S_1\unknown\cdots\unknown S_k\) such that each _S<sub>i</sub>_ is independent in _M_. Since _M_ is represented by _A_, for each \(i\in[k]\) there exists a subset \(R_i\subseteq[r]\) with |_R<sub>i</sub>_|=|_S<sub>i</sub>_| such that \(\mathrm{det}(A_{R_i,S_i})\neq 0\).

Let _R_ be the set of _s_ rows in _U_ formed by taking the rows corresponding to _R<sub>i</sub>_ from the _i_-th block _AC<sub>i</sub>_ (more formally, the set of the rows in _R_ is given by \(\{(i-1)r+j:i\in[k],j\in R_i\}\)).

Consider the \(s\times s\) square submatrix _U<sub>R,S</sub>_. By the generalized Laplace expansion (Lemma 2.6), on expanding along the _k_ row blocks _R_<sub>1</sub>_,...,R<sub>k</sub>_, det(_U<sub>R,S</sub>_) can be written as:

\(\mathrm{det}(U_{R,S})=\sum_{T_1\unknown\cdots\unknown T_k=S|T_i|=|R_i|}\pm\prod_{i=1}^k\mathrm{det}\big((AC_i)_{R_i,T_i}\big).\) (4)

For each _i_ and block _T<sub>i</sub>_, we can factor out the diagonal variables:

\(\mathrm{det}\big((AC_i)_{R_i,T_i}\big)=\mathrm{det}\big(A_{R_i,T_i}\big)\prod_{e\in T_i}c_{i,e},\)

where _c<sub>i,e</sub>_ denotes the (_e,e_) diagonal entry of the matrix _C<sub>i</sub>_.

For two distinct partitions (_T_<sub>1</sub>_,...,T<sub>k</sub>_) and \((T'_1,\dots,T'_k)\), the monomials \(\prod_{i\in[k]}\prod_{e\in T_i}c_{i,e}\) and \(\prod_{i\in[k]}\prod_{e\in T_i^\prime} c_{i,e}\) are distinct (since the variable indices (_i,e_) differ). Therefore, distinct partitions contribute linearly independent monomials, and det(_U<sub>R,S</sub>_) is a non-zero polynomial if at least one partition yields a non-zero coefficient. The partition (_S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>k</sub>_) contributes the coefficient \(\prod_{i=1}^k\mathrm{det}(A_{R_i,S_i})\neq 0\). Therefore, det(_U<sub>R,S</sub>_) is a non-zero polynomial.

Conversely, suppose the submatrix _U<sub>S</sub>_ has full column rank. Then det(_U<sub>R,S</sub>_) is a non-zero polynomial for some choice of rows \(R=R_1\unknown\cdots\unknown R_k\). By (4), there exists a partition (_T_<sub>1</sub>_,...,T<sub>k</sub>_) with \(\prod_{i=1}^k\mathrm{det}(A_{R_i,T_i})\neq 0\), implying each _T<sub>i</sub>_ is independent in _M_. Hence _S_ is independent in \(M^{\vee k}\).

If _S_ is independent in \(M^{\vee k}\), we have shown that _P<sub>S</sub>_:=det(_U<sub>R,S</sub>_) is a non-zero polynomial for some _R_. The degree of _P<sub>S</sub>_ is at most \(s\le kr\) (each variable appears with degree at most 1). By the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, under a uniformly random assignment from F to the variables:

\(Pr[P_S=0]\le\frac{deg(P_S)}{|\mathbb{F}|}\le\frac{kr}{|\mathbb{F}|}.\)

This proves the first claim as F is of size poly(_kr_). To establish the second claim, note that any set \(S\subseteq E\) which is dependent in \(M^{\vee k}\) yields the identically zero polynomial for all choices of _R_. So, such sets remain deterministically dependent under any field assignment. \(\square\)

## A.4 Extension of Perfect \(\alpha\)-factor Sensitivity Oracle to Maximum \(\alpha\)-factor

We extend the sensitivity oracle results of the (perfect) \(\alpha\)-factor (Theorems 7.8 and 8.13) to the (maximum) \(\alpha\)-factor, achieving near-identical bounds. Using the terminology from \[GS21a\], the (maximum) \(\alpha\)-factor treats \(\alpha(v)\) as an upper bound on the desired degree of _v_, and the objective is to maximize the total number of edges picked. In contrast, the (perfect) \(\alpha\)-factor treats \(\alpha(v)\) as the exact required degree for _v_, and the oracle strictly answers its existence.

Given a graph _G_=(_V,E_), the function \(\alpha\), edge costs \(c:E\rightarrow[-W,W]\), a precomputed min-cost (maximum) \(\alpha\)-factor _M_ of _G_, and a parameter _f\>_0, we first define the _deficiency def(v_) for any vertex \(v\in V\) as the difference between \(\alpha(v)\) and the number of edges incident to _v_ in _M_. Let \(\delta_M(v)\) denote the set of edges incident to _v_ in _M_. Hence, \(def(v)=\alpha(v)-|\delta_M(v)|\). By definition, \(def(v)\ge 0\).

We now construct an auxiliary undirected graph G from _G_ by adding three dummy vertices _z_<sub>1</sub>_,z_<sub>2</sub>_,z_<sub>3</sub>, along with the following sets of zero-cost edges:

• _E_<sub>_z_<sub>1</sub></sub>: For all \(v\in V\) , add _def(v_)+_f_ parallel edges between _z_<sub>1</sub> and _v_.<tbc>

• _E<sub>triangle</sub>_: Add _f_ parallel edges between each of the pairs (_z_<sub>1</sub>_,z_<sub>2</sub>),(_z_<sub>2</sub>_,z_<sub>3</sub>), and (_z_<sub>3</sub>_,z_<sub>1</sub>).

This yields the graph G=(V,E), where \(\mathcal{V}=V\cup\{z_1,z_2,z_3\}\) and \(\mathcal{E}=E\cup E_{z_1}\cup E_{triangle}\).

We now define a function \(\beta\) over the vertices of G as follows: \(\beta(z_1)=2f+\sum_{v\in V}def(v)\); \(\beta(z_2)=\beta(z_3)=2f\); and \(\beta(v)=\alpha(v)\) for all \(v\in V\) . By construction, G admits a (perfect) \(\beta\)-factor using a subset of the edges of _M_, _E_<sub>_z_<sub>1</sub></sub>, and _E<sub>triangle</sub>_. Furthermore, the cost of the min-cost maximum \(\alpha\)-factor of _G_ is exactly equal to the cost of the min-cost perfect \(\beta\)-factor of G.

For any set of edge updates _U_ in graph _G_, we describe the corresponding updates U to the graph G. For an update to any edge \(e\in G\), we apply the identical update to _e_ in G. We then augment the set U into a parameterized set U_<sup>i</sup>_ for \(i\in[-f,f]\) with the following additional dummy-edge updates:

• If _i\>_0: delete _i_ edges between _z_<sub>2</sub> and _z_<sub>3</sub>; add _i_ zero-cost edges between both (_z_<sub>1</sub>_,z_<sub>3</sub>) and (_z_<sub>1</sub>_,z_<sub>2</sub>).<tbc>

• If \(i\le 0\): add |_i_| zero-cost edges between _z_<sub>2</sub> and _z_<sub>3</sub>; delete |_i_| edges between both (_z_<sub>1</sub>_,z_<sub>3</sub>) and (_z_<sub>1</sub>_,z_<sub>2</sub>).

The following lemma establishes the equivalence between the two factors under these updates:

**Lemma A.3.** _The cardinality of the maximum_ \(\alpha\)_-factor of G+U is equal to_ |_M_|+_i_<sup>∗</sup>_, where i_<sup>∗</sup> _is the maximum possible integer_ \(i\in[-f,f]\) _such that the graph_ G+U_<sup>i</sup> admits a perfect_ \(\beta\)_-factor. Furthermore, the cost of the minimum-cost maximum_ \(\alpha\)_-factor of G+U is equal to the cost of the minimum-cost perfect_ \(\beta\)_-factor of_ G+U_<sup>i<sup>∗</sup></sup>.

_Proof._ Let \(M'\) be an arbitrary maximum \(\alpha\)-factor in _G+U_. Since _f_ updates can change the size of the maximum \(\alpha\)-factor by at most _f_, we know that \(|M|-f\le|M'|\le|M|+f\). Without loss of generality, we can assume that for all \(v\in V\) , the local change is bounded: \(\|\delta_M(v)|-|\delta_{M^\prime}(v)\|\le f\).

Observe that \(M'\) can be extended to a perfect \(\beta\)-factor _M<sub>i</sub>_ in \(\mathcal{G}+\mathcal{U}^i\), where \(i=|M'|-|M|\). This is achieved by picking exactly \(\sum_{v\in V}\alpha(v)-2|M'|\) edges from _E_<sub>_z_<sub>1</sub></sub> (which is always possible since \(\|\delta_M(v)|-|\delta_{M^\prime}(v)\|\le f\)). This leaves a remaining demand of \(2f+2(|M'|-|M|)\) at vertex _z_<sub>1</sub>, which must be strictly satisfied using edges from _E<sub>triangle</sub>_.

Since _z_<sub>2</sub> and _z_<sub>3</sub> have fixed capacities of 2_f_, this remaining demand uniquely forces _M<sub>i</sub>_ to pick exactly \(f+(|M'|-|M|)\) edges on both (_z_<sub>1</sub>_,z_<sub>2</sub>) and (_z_<sub>1</sub>_,z_<sub>3</sub>), and exactly \(f-(|M'|-|M|)\) edges on (_z_<sub>2</sub>_,z_<sub>3</sub>). This assignment forms a valid perfect \(\beta\)-factor in \(\mathcal{G}+\mathcal{U}^i\).

Thus, the maximum possible _i_ (denoted _i_<sup>∗</sup>) that yields a perfect \(\beta\)-factor in \(\mathcal{G}+\mathcal{U}^i\) perfectly corresponds to the maximum \(\alpha\)-factor of _G+U_. This proves the cardinality equivalence. Finally, because all dummy edges carry zero cost, the min-cost perfect \(\beta\)-factor strictly optimizes and matches the cost of the min-cost maximum \(\alpha\)-factor. □

We can now construct any perfect \(\beta\)-factor sensitivity oracle over the graph G. By Theorem A.3, this oracle resolves sensitivity queries for the maximum \(\alpha\)-factor in _G_. When an update **U** is queried, the optimal integer _i_<sup>∗</sup> can be found using a binary search over the interval \[-_f,f_\]. This binary search introduces a logarithmic overhead of _O_(log_f_), mapping the previous \(O(f^{3\omega})\) query time to \(\widetilde{O}(f^{3\omega})\).
